steps.title: Valves open and close the cylinder
steps.prompt:
Every cylinder breathes through two valves. The intake valve lets the fuel-air mixture in and the exhaust valve lets the burned gas out.

Over the four strokes each valve opens once. During compression and during the power stroke both valves stay shut, so the cylinder is sealed while the charge is squeezed and burned.

Each valve has three jobs: open at the right moment, stay open for the right length of time, and close at the right moment. Before you open the model, predict what pushes a valve open and what shuts it again.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 37 and 39: conventional poppet valves in the cylinder head, and the three requirements of the valve-operating mechanism (open at the proper time, stay open for the required length of time, close at the proper time). Both valves closed during the compression and power strokes: Figure 1-36, PDF p. 47. The prediction is answered in the steps that follow.

mediaPlan.rationale: A prediction prompt: the learner commits to an idea before the mechanism is shown.

steps.title: Valves, seats and guides
steps.prompt: Find the [intake valve](IntakeValve) and the [exhaust valve](ExhaustValve) in the cylinder head. Each valve is a head on a long stem. The face of the head closes on a hard seat insert in its port, and the stem slides in a guide that keeps it square to the seat. These are poppet valves: they lift straight off the seat to open.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 38 (the ground valve face seals on the valve seat; the stem acts as a pilot in the valve guide) and the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 16 (seats and guides are installed in the heated head before it is screwed and shrunk onto the barrel; the exhaust valves are faced with a heat- and corrosion-resistant material and the solid stem tips are hardened). The cylinder is a teaching reconstruction of the GTSIO-520-H cylinder (reviewed release): part shapes and the motions are illustrative.

mediaPlan.rationale: The cylinder model shows where the valves, seats and guides sit relative to the head and ports.

steps.title: Valve shapes and metals
steps.prompt: Valves are named for their shape: mushroom, tulip and semi-tulip. They work in heat, corrosion and constant hammering, so the metal matters. Intake valves run cooler and can be chromic-nickel steel. Exhaust valves run hotter and are made of nichrome, silchrome or cobalt-chromium steel. Some stems are hollow and part filled with metallic sodium (the sodium chamber in the figure). Sodium melts at about 208 °F (98 °C) and sloshes as the valve moves, carrying heat from the head up the stem to the guide, which can cool the valve by 300 to 400 °F. Never cut open or scrap a sodium-filled valve as ordinary metal: sodium exposed to air or water burns or explodes.
steps.alt: FAA figure of six valve types (hollow-head mushroom, mushroom and tulip, then tulip, semi-tulip and tulip), with labels for the sodium chamber, large and small stems, hardened tip, face, neck and head.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 38-39 (valve shapes, intake and exhaust valve materials, sodium-filled stems, the 300 to 400 °F cooling and the warning about cutting open a sodium valve). The course deck gives the melting point as 97.5 °C; the handbook gives approximately 208 °F, which is about 98 °C.

mediaPlan.rationale: The handbook figure names every part of a valve and shows each shape side by side.

steps.title: Springs, retainers and keepers
steps.prompt: Each valve is closed by two springs, one inside the other. A single spring would vibrate, or surge, at certain engine speeds. Two springs surge at different speeds, so they damp each other, and they are less likely to break from heat and fatigue. The springs sit under a retainer that is locked to the stem by tapered half-round keepers (split keys), which fit a groove cut near the tip of the stem. On the exhaust valve the retainer is a Rotocoil type. The springs close the valve, hold it on its seat and push the whole valve train back the other way.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 38 and 42 (stem keys and the groove in the stem; two or three springs, spring surge, and the springs closing the valve and holding it on its seat), cross-checked against EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 62-63, and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 16 (outer spring retainers are locked to the stems by tapered, semi-circular keys) and p. 58 (the exhaust side has a rotocap). The model's description of the Rotocoil (it promotes small valve rotations that spread heat and wear) is not stated on the manual pages read here. The cylinder is a teaching reconstruction of the GTSIO-520-H cylinder (reviewed release): part shapes and the motions are illustrative.

mediaPlan.rationale: The exploded pose separates the springs, retainer and keepers so each can be named.

steps.title: Cam lobe and ramps
steps.prompt: A valve lifts only when a cam lobe pushes. The shape of the lobe sets the valve lift (how far the valve leaves its seat) and the valve duration (how long it stays open). Look for the ramp on each side of the lobe: it eases the rocker arm into contact with the valve tip, so the shock is much smaller than if the parts met a sharp edge. The round part of the cam, away from the nose, is the base circle. While the follower rides the base circle the valve is closed.
steps.alt: FAA figure of a cam lobe seen end-on on its camshaft, and a side view of the lobe profile with the cam ramps marked on both flanks.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 39 (valve lift and duration are determined by the shape of the cam lobes; the ramp or step on each side of the lobe) and PDF p. 41 (the tappet body rests on the base circle, or back, of the cam when the valve is closed), cross-checked against EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 58-59.

mediaPlan.rationale: The handbook figure labels the cam ramps, which the interactive that follows then shows in motion.

steps.title: Lift and duration
steps.prompt: Turn the crank and watch the tappet ride the cam. Then choose the other lobe shapes. How does the taller lobe change the lift? How does the longer lobe change the time the valve stays open? Notice that one turn of the cam covers two turns of the crank.
steps.note: Schematic interactive made for this lesson. Lift and duration follow FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 39 (set by the shape of the cam lobes; ramps on each flank). The standard lobe copies the intake valve of the FAA example timing chart (Figure 1-37, PDF p. 47: opens 50° before TDC, closes 30° after BDC); the other two are invented for contrast. None of the lobes is GTSIO-520-H cam data, and lift is in relative units, not millimetres.

mediaPlan.rationale: Choosing a lobe and turning the crank makes lift and duration something the learner changes, not just reads.

steps.title: Why the cam turns at half speed
steps.prompt: A valve opens once in every four-stroke cycle, and a cycle takes two turns of the crankshaft. So the camshaft turns once for every two turns of the crankshaft. The cam gear is twice the size of the crankshaft gear, so it runs at half the speed. Find the crankshaft gear, the larger timing gear on the camshaft and the lobes on the camshaft.
steps.alt: FAA drawing of a small crankshaft gear driving a gear twice its size on the camshaft, with the camshaft lobes labelled and a note that the cam gear runs at half speed.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 41 (the camshaft of an opposed engine always rotates at one-half the crankshaft speed; Figure 1-28: the cam gear is twice the size of the crankshaft gear), cross-checked against EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 60-61. The GTSIO-520 gear train (overhaul manual, PDF p. 17 and Figure A-4-8, PDF p. 25) also drives the camshaft gear directly from the crankshaft gear. The two-to-one reasoning is the learner-level explanation; the handbook states the ratio.

mediaPlan.rationale: The handbook figure shows the gear pair and the lobes in one drawing.

steps.title: The camshaft in the GTSIO-520-H
steps.prompt: In the GTSIO-520-H the camshaft lies inside the crankcase, so this view shows it on its own with the gears of its drive. A gear on its rear end meshes with the crankshaft gear. The camshaft is a hardened and ground steel-alloy forging with four journals and nine lobes. Its gear is bolted on with four unequally spaced bolts so that its timing mark sits in the right place relative to the lobes.
steps.note: Documented from the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 17 (section A-3-1 h: four journals, nine cam lobes, gear mount flange at the rear end, four unequally spaced bolts to locate the timing mark in relation to the cam lobes) and the gear train in Figure A-4-8, PDF p. 25. The full-engine model is a teaching reconstruction: what is visible through the crankcase is illustrative.

mediaPlan.rationale: The whole-engine model places the camshaft inside the crankcase relative to the cylinders.

steps.title: From cam to valve
steps.prompt: Trace the motion for the [intake valve](IntakeValve). The cam lobe lifts the [tappet](IntakeHydraulicLifterBody). The tappet moves the [pushrod](IntakePushrod), which runs in a tube from the crankcase to the cylinder head. The pushrod tips the [rocker arm](IntakeRockerArm) on [its shaft](IntakeRockerShaft), and the other end of the rocker arm presses the valve stem and opens the valve. When the lobe passes, the valve spring closes the valve and pushes everything back. Engine oil takes a path too: it reaches the rocker arm through the hollow pushrod and returns to the crankcase through the [pushrod housing](IntakePushrodHousing).
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 39 and 42 (cam follower, push rod and ball socket, rocker arm, valve; the hollow pushrod carries engine oil to the rocker assembly), cross-checked against EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 59-62, and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 16 (oil is forced through the pushrods to the drilled rockers and returns to the crankcase through the pushrod housings). The cylinder model has no camshaft: the tappet body stands for the end of the train that meets the cam. The cylinder is a teaching reconstruction of the GTSIO-520-H cylinder (reviewed release): part shapes and the motions are illustrative.

mediaPlan.rationale: The exploded valve-train stage separates the tappet, pushrod, rocker arm and valve so the order can be traced.

steps.title: The opposed-engine valve train
steps.prompt: Here is the whole valve train of an opposed engine in one picture: the camshaft in the crankcase, the tappet, the pushrod, and the rocker arm and valve spring up in the cylinder head. The GTSIO-520-H is built this way. The figure is a general example, not a GTSIO-520-H drawing.
steps.alt: FAA cutaway of an opposed engine cylinder and crankcase with the camshaft, tappet and push rod in the crankcase and the valve spring in the cylinder head labelled.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 39-41 (the valve mechanism of an opposed engine is operated by a camshaft; Figure 1-25), cross-checked against EASA Module 16, PDF p. 60. The GTSIO-520 layout is described in its overhaul manual, PDF pp. 16-17 (camshaft and hydraulic tappets in the crankcase, pushrods, rocker arms on the cylinder heads).

mediaPlan.rationale: A single cutaway shows how far the motion travels from the crankcase to the head.

steps.title: Radial engines use a cam ring
steps.prompt: A radial engine has no camshaft. A cam ring, a steel ring with lobes, turns around the crankshaft. It has one track of lobes for the intake valves and one for the exhaust valves. Cam rollers ride the tracks and lift the tappets in their guides, and the motion goes on through the pushrod and rocker arm to the valve, as in an opposed engine. The crankshaft drives the ring at a much lower speed. On a nine-cylinder engine a four-lobe ring turns the opposite way to the crankshaft. Compare this figure with the opposed engine.
steps.alt: FAA drawing of the valve-operating mechanism of a radial engine: a cam ring with cam track and lobe, a cam roller, tappet and tappet guide, a push rod tube, and the rocker arm, valve spring and valve guide in the cylinder head.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 39-41 (cam rings; one ring with a double cam track on a single-row radial; driven by the crankshaft at a reduced speed; the four-lobe ring on a nine-cylinder engine turns opposite to the crankshaft; Figures 1-24 and 1-27), cross-checked against EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 59-60.

mediaPlan.rationale: The handbook drawing is the clearest labelled picture of a cam ring and its tracks.

steps.title: Why a ring, and why it turns slowly
steps.prompt:
A radial engine's cylinders spread like spokes around the crankshaft, in one plane. A straight camshaft would run alongside only some of them. A cam ring turns around the crankshaft itself, so it passes the same distance from every cylinder, and each cylinder's tappet can ride on it.

The ring turns slowly. A valve must open once in every two crankshaft turns, and a ring with L lobes on a track lifts each valve L times per turn. So the ring turns at 1 / (2 × L) of crankshaft speed: with four lobes, one eighth.

The handbook table agrees in all six entries. A nine-cylinder engine with a four-lobe ring runs it at 1/8 speed, against the crankshaft; with five lobes, at 1/10, with the crankshaft.

One lobe serves several cylinders in turn, so the ring needs fewer lobes than there are cylinders.
steps.alt: Table of radial-engine cam rings for 5, 7 and 9 cylinders, giving the number of lobes and the ring speed as a fraction of crankshaft speed. Turning with the crankshaft: 3 lobes at 1/6, 4 lobes at 1/8 and 5 lobes at 1/10. Turning opposite the crankshaft: 2 lobes at 1/4, 3 lobes at 1/6 and 4 lobes at 1/8.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 39 to 41: the ring is mounted concentrically with the crankshaft and driven by it at a reduced speed; one ring with a double track in a single-row radial; a four-lobe ring on a nine-cylinder engine turns opposite to the crankshaft; Figure 1-27, the cam ring table (PDF p. 41). The rule speed = 1 / (2 × lobes) is the lesson's explanation, from the four-stroke cycle (one valve opening per two crankshaft turns); it fits every entry of Figure 1-27. The reason a straight camshaft will not do is also the lesson's reasoning from the arrangement; the handbook describes the ring and does not argue the point. Twin-row radials use a second ring.

mediaPlan.rationale: The handbook table makes the lobes-to-speed relationship visible, and the reader can test the rule against every entry.

steps.title: The zero-lash tappet
steps.prompt: A solid tappet leaves a small gap in the valve train, the valve clearance, which must be adjusted by hand. A hydraulic tappet takes up the gap by itself. Engine oil from the lubrication system fills a chamber under the plunger. When the cam pushes the tappet body, a check valve closes and traps the oil, and the trapped oil carries the load to the pushrod almost like a solid link. Find the plunger, the plunger spring, the check valve and the two oil chambers. The figure shows a ball check valve; the GTSIO-520 tappet uses a spring-loaded check-valve plate instead.
steps.alt: FAA cutaway of a hydraulic valve tappet beside a cam, with the tappet body, plunger, plunger spring, ball check valve, cylinder, oil supply chamber, oil pressure chamber, push rod socket, push rod and shroud tube labelled.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 41-42 (solid lifters need the valve clearance adjusted by hand; hydraulic tappets keep the clearance at zero; the oil in the pressure chamber acts as a cushion; a predetermined leakage between plunger and cylinder bore compensates for expansion and contraction), cross-checked against EASA Module 16, PDF p. 61. The GTSIO-520 tappet (overhaul manual, Figure A-4-10, PDF p. 27) lists a check-valve plate, check-valve spring and housing, not a ball.

mediaPlan.rationale: The labelled cutaway names the oil chambers and the check valve before the model shows them move.

steps.title: Trapped oil under load
steps.prompt: The tappet body is faint here, so you can see the parts inside it at the moment when the load is on: the closed check valve keeps the oil in the chamber, and the trapped oil carries the load. Open Explore to play the whole cycle. When the valve closes, the [plunger spring](PlungerSpring) extends the [plunger](Plunger) and oil flows back in. A small controlled leak past the plunger lets the tappet follow the expansion and contraction of the valve train. For a closer look, open the Inside the hydraulic tappet study in the Internal Mechanisms course.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 42 and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, Figure A-4-10, PDF p. 27 (items 1-16). Manual relationships; the dimensions and the operating travel are illustrative, and the model is not a pressure simulation or a maintenance procedure.

mediaPlan.rationale: The tappet study shows the plunger, check plate and oil path moving through one illustrative cycle.

steps.title: Valve clearance and why it matters
steps.prompt: Solid tappets need valve clearance: a small gap so the valve can close completely when the parts expand with heat. On those engines the clearance must be checked and adjusted. Wrong clearance changes the real valve timing. With too much clearance the valves do not open as wide or stay open as long, so the overlap is shorter. With too little, the overlap is longer. Overlap affects the idle mixture, and clearances are never wrong by the same amount in every cylinder, so the mixture differs from cylinder to cylinder. Hydraulic tappets remove most of this work. They are not maintenance-free: they work only over a limited range and can stick.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 41 (solid lifters and valve clearance) and PDF pp. 401-403 (operational effect of valve clearance on valve overlap and idle mixture, variation between cylinders, and the limited range and sticking of hydraulic lifters). The handbook text and the caption of its Figure 10-51 describe the mixture direction in opposite ways, so this step does not state a direction.

mediaPlan.rationale: A cause-and-effect step that builds on the overlap diagram from the Thermodynamic Cycles lesson.

steps.title: Timing the cam to the crank
steps.prompt:
Valve timing is the relationship between the camshaft and the crankshaft: at which crank angles each lobe lifts its valve.

It is set when the engine is built, by meshing the camshaft gear with the crankshaft gear so that their timing marks line up. The timing itself, the lead, lag and overlap you will meet next, comes from where the lobes sit on the cam and where the cam gear sits on the camshaft.

Real timing values come from the engine manufacturer. The FAA chart in the next steps is an example, not GTSIO-520-H timing.
steps.note: Documented from the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 77 (section 12-4: mesh the camshaft spur gear with the crankshaft gear so that the timing marks align, Figure A4-35) and PDF p. 17 (the camshaft gear is bolted on to locate its timing mark relative to the lobes). The manual searched here gives no valve timing figures; the FAA example chart is in FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 47, Figure 1-37.

mediaPlan.rationale: A short linking step: valve timing is a gear-timing relationship, shown earlier by the timing chart.

steps.title: Valve lead, lag and overlap
steps.prompt:
Valve timing is given in degrees of crankshaft travel. It marks when a valve starts to open or finishes closing, not when it is fully open.

Valve lead: a valve opens before the piston reaches the end of its stroke. The intake valve opens before TDC, near the end of the exhaust stroke. The exhaust valve opens before BDC, near the end of the power stroke.

Valve lag: a valve closes after the piston has passed the end of its stroke. The exhaust valve closes after TDC. The intake valve closes after BDC, on the compression stroke.

Valve overlap: around TDC, at the start of the intake stroke, the intake valve has opened and the exhaust valve has not yet closed, so both are off their seats at once.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 46 to 48: timing is specified in degrees of crankshaft travel and gives the start of opening, not the full-open position (p. 47); the intake valve opens before TDC on the exhaust stroke (valve lead); the exhaust valve closes after TDC (valve lag); both valves are off their seats at TDC at the start of the intake stroke (valve overlap); the intake valve closes after BDC on the compression stroke; the exhaust valve opens before BDC on the power stroke (p. 48). The terms lead and lag for the exhaust opening and the intake closing follow the same sense (early and late) and are the lesson's wording.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Why open early and close late
steps.prompt:
Opening early and closing late looks wasteful. It pays because moving gas has momentum and a cylinder has very little time.

Intake lead: the exhaust gas leaving the cylinder leaves a low pressure behind, which speeds the fresh charge in as the valve starts to open. It opens 8° to 55° before TDC on various engines.

Intake lag: near BDC the piston hardly moves, so the charge keeps flowing in after BDC. The valve closes about 50° to 75° after BDC.

Exhaust lead: opening well before BDC lets the pressure left in the cylinder push the gas out and carry waste heat away.

Overlap cools the cylinder with cool incoming charge, draws in more mixture and clears the burned gas.

Too much lead lets hot gas flash back; too much lag forces gas back out.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 47 (the intake valve is opened before TDC to induce more charge; the limit is hot gas flashing back; overlap aids internal cooling, charge and scavenging; the intake valve closes about 50 to 75 degrees past BDC so that the momentum of the incoming gas charges the cylinder, and too late forces gas back through the valve) and PDF p. 48 (the speed of the leaving exhaust gas creates a low pressure that speeds the fresh charge in; intake opening at 8 to 55 degrees before TDC on various engines; the exhaust valve opens considerably before BDC, on some engines at 50 or 75 degrees, so that pressure forces the gases out and frees the cylinder of waste heat). Why the piston barely moves near BDC: the lesson's wording of the handbook's remark that the slight upward travel near BDC has little effect on the incoming flow.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 47, Figure 1-37 (valve timing chart: start of the cycle 50 degrees BTC with the intake valve opening; intake valve closes 30 degrees ABC; exhaust valve opens 30 degrees BBC; finish of the cycle 25 degrees ATC with the exhaust valve closed; valve overlap 75 degrees, both valves open) and its text: the valve events vary considerably in different engines and the manufacturer's recommendations must be followed. The chart values are an FAA example, not GTSIO-520-H timing; the GTSIO-520 manual searched here gives no valve timing figures. The sums are the lesson's reading of the chart: 180 degrees is one stroke.

mediaPlan.rationale: The handbook chart is a real timing diagram; reading its four events and adding the angles is the skill this lesson asks for.

steps.title: Try the chart yourself
steps.prompt:
Now check the reading on the moving chart. Drag the crank angle through the whole 720°.

Find the four events A to D. At what angle does the overlap begin, and at what angle does it end? During which two strokes does the chart show both valves shut for the whole stroke?
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 47, Figure 1-37 (example valve timing chart) and its text: valve events vary considerably in different engines, and the manufacturer's recommendations must be followed. The chart values are an FAA example, not GTSIO-520-H timing; the GTSIO-520 manual searched here gives no valve timing figures. The same interactive appears in Thermodynamic Cycles; here it checks the reading made in the previous step.

mediaPlan.rationale: A crank-angle marker over a two-revolution timeline shows valve state and overlap at any angle, so the sums from the chart can be checked.

steps.title: Inspecting a valve
steps.prompt: At overhaul each valve is inspected. Check the face and the tip for pitting and wear, the stem for stretch (a smaller diameter near the neck) and wear in its guide, and look for cracks, nicks, burning or corrosion: a valve with burn or corrosion damage is not reused. The face must run true with the stem within 0.0015 in. After a valve is ground, check the margin, the thickness of its edge. A thin feather edge overheats, can cause pre-ignition and burns away quickly. If the edge is thinner than the manufacturer's limit after re-facing, the valve is not reused.
steps.alt: FAA drawing of two valve heads: one with a normal margin, the thickness of the edge of the head, and one ground to a thin feather edge.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 379-380 (valve inspection: face and tip, stretch and wear, damage from burning or corrosion; Figure 10-12: face must run true with the stem within 0.0015 inch; edge thickness limit set by the manufacturer) and PDF p. 384 (feather edge, pre-ignition, Figure 10-26). The course deck also quotes a 1/32 in minimum margin, which the handbook pages read here do not give: use the manufacturer's limit.

mediaPlan.rationale: The drawing shows what a normal margin and a feather edge look like.

steps.title: Checking a valve spring
steps.prompt: Valve springs are checked for cracks, rust and broken ends, and for compression. A spring tester compresses the spring to a set height and its dial shows the force in pounds. The force must be within the manufacturer's limits. The GTSIO-520 overhaul manual's table of limits lists, for the inner spring (P/N 637836): at 1.329 in, a serviceable limit of 73 lb (new springs 78 to 88 lb); at 1.809 in, 40 lb (new 43 to 49 lb). For the outer spring (P/N 637837): at 1.275 in, 118 lb (new 126 to 140 lb); at 1.791 in, 46 lb (new 49 to 55 lb). A spring that pushes back with less than the serviceable limit at the test height is not reused. These are numbers for the springs that manual lists. Always use the data for the engine in front of you.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 379-381 (examine springs for cracks, rust, broken ends and compression; the spring is compressed to the height the manufacturer specifies and the pressure must be within the manufacturer's limits) and the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, Table of Limits, spring test data, PDF p. 95 (page B-4, March 1981). The chapter for the -H (C-3) lists no different valve spring. The values are teaching data from that manual edition, not a maintenance instruction.

mediaPlan.rationale: The numbers in the manual table are the evidence; a picture would add nothing.

steps.title: Cam, tappets and what gets replaced
steps.prompt: Inspect the camshaft lobes for scoring, corrosion and overheating, and for pitting at the toes. Clean and inspect each hydraulic tappet: a body with damage on its cam-follower face, deep scoring or corrosion is discarded. A quick dry test checks the plunger. Press it in and release it, and it should kick back, because trapped air is compressed. If it does not return fully, the plunger is worn or the check valve is leaking. The overhaul manual recommends replacing every valve spring, valve keeper, exhaust valve and Rotocoil, and all hydraulic lifters, at each major overhaul, whatever their condition. If lifters are removed early they must go back where they came from.
steps.note: Documented from the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual: PDF p. 66 (9-15, camshaft lobe inspection), PDF pp. 67 and 84-86 (9-20 and 13-1 to 13-5, hydraulic lifter inspection and the dry plunger kick-back test), PDF p. 72 (10-12, parts replaced 100 percent at normal major overhaul, and the note that lifters removed early go back in the same location) and PDF p. 58 (7-15, lifters recommended to be replaced at each major overhaul). This is a recognition lesson, not a service procedure: the manual gives the steps.

mediaPlan.rationale: The inspection and replacement rules are the evidence and need no picture.

steps.title: Trace the whole path
steps.prompt:
Explain the whole path in your own words, starting at the crankshaft gear and ending with the valve closing again. Which parts move, and how fast does the camshaft turn? Why does a radial use a ring?

Then explain the timing. What do valve lead, lag and overlap mean, and why do they help the engine breathe? What does a hydraulic tappet do about clearance? Which parts would you inspect, and what would you look for?

Then take the lesson's quiz.
steps.note: Completion step: the learner pulls the lesson together (opening prompt, action, feedback, completion evidence) from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 37 to 42, 47 to 48 and 379 to 384, and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF pp. 16 to 17 and 66 to 67.

mediaPlan.rationale: The learner explains the path in their own words.

lessons.title: Accessories & Drives
lessons.objective: Identify accessories and interfaces, trace power paths, predict rotation, operate saved motions and explain useful functions and illustrative faults.
lessons.purpose: Show that the crankshaft does much more than simply turn the propeller.
outcomes: Explain why an operating aircraft engine requires a range of mechanically driven accessories.
Trace mechanical power from the crankshaft to the accessory section.
Identify common engine-driven accessories.
State the functions of common accessories including magnetos, oil pumps, fuel pumps, tachometer drives and propeller-governor drives.
Recognise alternators/generators, vacuum pumps and other possible accessory loads.
Identify components commonly mounted on the accessory housing.
Explain how an accessory gearbox distributes mechanical power.
Describe the operation and application of spur gears.
Describe the operation and application of bevel gears.
Explain the purpose of a propeller reduction gear and shaft.
Explain why some engines use reduction gearing while others drive the propeller directly.
Distinguish wet-sump and dry-sump arrangements.
Recognise how accessory-drive failure could affect continued engine operation.
lessons.syllabusNote: The formal module explicitly requires propeller reduction gearing, bevel gears, spur gears, wet/dry sump arrangements and accessory-housing components.
lessons.completionCriteria: Explain why an engine needs mechanically driven accessories, name the common ones and say what each does, and trace one full drive path from the crankshaft gear to the accessory; use the tooth counts of a spur gear pair to find a speed and a direction, and say what bevel gears and an idler are for; explain why some engines use reduction gearing and others drive the propeller directly; tell a wet-sump system from a dry-sump system; say what follows when an accessory drive fails; and calculate a verified ratio with the correct viewpoint, inspect a section and tell evidence from illustration on the model.

steps.title: Where power goes
steps.prompt:
A turning crankshaft does more than turn the propeller. Some of its power keeps the engine itself alive: the magnetos that make the spark, and the pumps that move oil and fuel. Some of it serves the aircraft: electricity, suction for instruments and propeller control.

These engine-driven devices are the accessories, and almost all of them take their power mechanically, through gears.

Before you read on, predict: which devices need shaft power? And one device must put power into the engine before it can run. Which one?
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 28 (the accessory section carries mounting pads for magnetos, fuel, oil and vacuum pumps, starter, generator and tachometer drive; gear trains drive the engine's accessories at the proper speeds) and the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF pp. 17 to 18 (the gear train from the crankshaft gear to the accessories, and the starter drive). The prediction is answered in the steps that follow.

mediaPlan.rationale: A prediction prompt frames the lesson; the model steps that follow answer it.

steps.title: The accessories and what they do
steps.prompt:
Magnetos make the spark, one for each of the two ignition systems.

The oil pump pushes oil to the bearings under pressure. The fuel pump delivers fuel under pressure to the fuel system.

The tachometer drive turns the tachometer, which shows crankshaft rpm.

The propeller governor drive spins the governor, which uses engine oil to change the blade angle and hold the propeller speed.

The alternator or generator makes electricity for the aircraft. A vacuum pump makes suction for instruments, on aircraft that have one.

The starter works the other way: it puts torque into the crankshaft until the engine runs.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 28 (accessories mounted on the accessory section: magnetos, fuel, oil and vacuum pumps, starter, generator and tachometer drive), PDF p. 84 (the engine fuel system includes the engine-driven pumps), PDF p. 391 (the tachometer for reciprocating engines shows crankshaft rpm), PDF pp. 27 and 294 (the propeller governor controls speed and blade angle with oil) and PDF p. 468 (dual ignition: two spark plugs in each cylinder, with two of every critical unit). The vacuum pump's use for gyro instruments, on older systems, is from the course deck (slide 'Various Aircraft Engine Accessories'); the GTSIO-520-H lists vacuum, de-icing and autopilot drives as options (reviewed manual, H section C-3-3).

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: The accessory section
steps.prompt:
Everything above bolts onto the accessory section, the rear part of the crankcase assembly. It is usually an aluminium alloy casting, sometimes magnesium, and it carries the mounting pads where the accessories fit. Find the magneto, generator, starter, oil pump and tachometer generator in the figure.

Drive shafts carry power out to the pads. A gear train inside the accessory case takes the power from the crankshaft and hands it to each shaft at its own speed: one source, many outputs. The gear ratios are chosen to give each accessory the right speed, for example the speed at which the magnetos give correct spark timing.

The accessory section is a small gearbox.
steps.alt: FAA exploded view of a typical opposed engine broken into its component assemblies: the two crankcase halves, crankshaft, camshaft, connecting rod and cylinder, with the accessory case assembly at the rear carrying the generator, magneto, tachometer generator, starter and oil pump, and the oil sump below.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 28 and Figure 1-6: the accessory (rear) section, usually cast aluminium alloy or sometimes magnesium, provided with means for mounting the accessories; accessory drive shafts carried out to the mounting pads; various gear ratios arranged to give the proper drive speed to magnetos, pumps and other accessories to obtain correct timing or functioning. The same figure is used in Parts and Construction.

mediaPlan.rationale: The exploded figure names the accessories and shows the accessory case at the rear of the engine.

steps.title: Identify the section
steps.prompt: Rotate the assembled study. Select the [housing](AccessoryHousing), [crank gear](CrankGear), [cam gear](CamGear) and [idler](IdlerGear). Open Inside and move a section plane through the chamber; distinguish solid wall from empty cavity.
steps.note: FAA 1-7; GTSIO A-3-2 and A-4-8 (PDF 17,25). A-4-18 (PDF 35-36) identifies the split crankcase. Compare its rear region with the cropped case halves here. Adapter, starter and pump forms follow the parts drawings, while rear contour, proportions and pad positions remain inferred. Ring markers are not accessory bodies.

mediaPlan.rationale: The assembled study lets the learner find the housing, crank gear, cam gear and idler, and see inside the case with the section plane.

steps.title: Spur gears
steps.prompt:
A spur gear has straight teeth cut parallel to its shaft. Two spur gears mesh on parallel shafts, and their teeth roll against each other like two wheels that cannot slip. So the rims move at the same speed, and the gear with fewer teeth turns faster.

Speed of the driven gear = speed of the driver × driver teeth ÷ driven teeth.

The 14-tooth gear in the picture must turn twice to turn the 28-tooth gear once: the speed ratio is 1 : 2, and the big gear runs at half speed. The two gears turn in opposite directions.

The handbook says spur gears generally drive the heavier loaded accessories, and those that need the least play, called backlash, in the gear train.
steps.alt: Two meshing spur gears: a smaller red gear with 14 teeth on the left drives a larger green gear with 28 teeth on the right, each with a round hub.
steps.credit: Jahobr, Two spur gears 1 2.svg, Wikimedia Commons
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 28: gear trains containing both spur and bevel gears drive the engine's accessories; spur-type gears are generally used to drive the heavier loaded accessories or those requiring the least play or backlash in the gear train. The speed rule (rim speeds equal, so speed is inversely proportional to teeth) is standard gear kinematics and is the lesson's explanation. Picture: 'Two spur gears 1:2' by Jahobr, released under CC0 (Wikimedia Commons, File:Two spur gears 1 2.svg; checked 13 October 2026): 14 teeth and 28 teeth.

mediaPlan.rationale: A labelled pair of meshing gears makes the tooth-ratio rule visible before the learner tries it.

steps.title: Try the gear explorer
steps.prompt:
Choose a driver and a driven gear, then turn the driver. Which gear turns faster, and by how much?

Try a 12-tooth driver and a 36-tooth driven gear: how many turns of the driver make one turn of the driven gear?

Now add the idler. Which way does the driven gear turn, and does its speed change?
steps.note: Schematic interactive made for this lesson. The speed rule (driven speed = driver speed × driver teeth ÷ driven teeth) is standard gear kinematics; each external mesh reverses the direction of rotation, so one idler restores the driver's direction without changing the ratio. The gear sizes and tooth shapes are drawn to show the rule, not taken from any engine's gear train. The idler is the idea behind the GTSIO-520 gear train, in which the crankshaft gear drives an idler gear that drives the magneto drive gears (overhaul manual, PDF p. 17).

mediaPlan.rationale: Choosing tooth counts and turning the driver shows the ratio, the speeds and the direction change at once, and the idler toggle shows why an idler does not change the ratio.

steps.title: Bevel gears
steps.prompt:
A bevel gear has its teeth cut on a cone instead of a cylinder. Two bevel gears can drive each other with their shafts meeting at an angle, usually 90°. The picture shows a pair with curved teeth, called spiral bevel gears.

On an engine this lets a drive turn a corner. The handbook says bevel gears permit angular location of short stub shafts leading to the accessory mounting pads.

In the GTSIO-520 the propeller governor is driven this way: a bevel gear on the front of the camshaft turns a driven bevel gear that drives the governor. The course slides add the mechanical tachometer drive, which also turns through 90°.

Spur gears keep a drive on parallel shafts. Bevel gears turn it.
steps.alt: A pair of spiral bevel gears: a small conical pinion on a splined shaft meshes at a right angle with a large ring gear, both with curved teeth.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 28: bevel gears permit angular location of short stub shafts leading to the various accessory mounting pads. The governor drive bevel gear on the front of the camshaft driving the governor driven bevel gear: Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 17 (section A-3-2 a). Bevel gears for the propeller governor and mechanical tachometer drives, through 90 degrees: course deck, slide 'Accessory Gear Trains' (tier 4, not found in the manual pages read here). Picture: 'Bevel gear (toothed wheels)' by Myriam Thyes, in the public domain (Wikimedia Commons, File:Gear-kegelzahnrad.svg; checked 13 October 2026); the pair shown has spiral teeth.

mediaPlan.rationale: A picture of a bevel pair shows the cone-shaped teeth and the right-angle meeting of the shafts.

steps.title: Expose interfaces
steps.prompt: Scrub from assembled to exploded. Pause at any stage, rotate and select a seal, splined shaft, bored adapter and coupling. Compare the adapter with A-4-11 and starter with A-4-15; identify one visible feature and one reconstructed surface. Explain which part carries torque and which contains oil or locates the accessory.
steps.note: GTSIO A-4-11 (PDF 28), A-4-15 (32), A-4-16 (33). Separation order and distances teach relationships; they are not maintenance instructions.

mediaPlan.rationale: The exploded stages let the learner see which part carries torque and which seals or locates the accessory.

steps.title: Trace magneto power
steps.prompt: Choose Magnetos under Trace power path, then isolate the complete path. Follow crank → idler → both drive gears → splined shafts → magnetos. Predict the idler direction before playing.
steps.note: A-3-2; A-4-8; H C-3-2 (PDF 152): both magneto drives 1.5:1, CW facing engine drive pad. The mesh tooth counts are illustrative; the 1.5 output ratio is verified.

mediaPlan.rationale: The magneto power path is isolated on the model so the learner can follow crank gear, idler, drive gears and splined shafts.

steps.title: Mechanical to ignition
steps.prompt:
Follow each magneto to the upper and lower spark plugs. Explain how shaft rotation becomes timed spark energy.

Why two magnetos and two plugs per cylinder? Dual ignition has two of every critical unit. It gives safety if one system fails, and, more important, lighting the charge in two places burns it more efficiently.
steps.alt: Manufacturer GTSIO-520 dual ignition wiring figure
steps.credit: Continental GTSIO-520 Figure A4-43; existing course extract
steps.note: FAA PDF 160-162 (4-1 to 4-3): magnet, primary and secondary circuits. H C-3-2 lists two magnetos and twelve plugs. This is two magnetos, not a single dual-magneto housing. Dual ignition: two of every critical unit, including two spark plugs in each cylinder; safety if one system fails and, more important, more efficient combustion from igniting the charge at two locations: FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), glossary, PDF p. 468.

mediaPlan.rationale: The GTSIO-520 ignition wiring diagram shows the two magnetos and the upper and lower spark plugs.

steps.title: Timing and viewpoint
steps.prompt: The H table gives 20° BTC for both magnetos. A drive speed ratio alone does not set ignition timing. Explain why a drive described as clockwise will appear counterclockwise when you view it from the opposite end.
steps.note: H C-3-2 to C-3-3 (PDF 152-153). Accessory CW/CCW is facing the engine drive pad. Propeller CW is looking forward, with 0.667:1 propeller/crank ratio; do not use propeller RPM as crank RPM. No timing adjustment procedure is prescribed.

mediaPlan.rationale: A written reasoning prompt about timing data and viewpoint.

steps.title: Fuel delivery
steps.prompt: Select the Fuel path. Find the [cluster gear](CamCluster), [pump drive gear](FuelGear) and [detachable coupling](FuelCoupling). Scrub the focused motion. Explain how loss of torque at the coupling could interrupt engine-driven fuel delivery.
steps.note: A-3-2; H C-3-6 (PDF 156): later pump replacement needs a changed drive gear and coupling; older installation differs. Fuel-drive ratio and rotation are unverified here; tooth sizes and motion are illustrative. Fuel pump internals are omitted. FAA PDF 84 (2-2) explains reciprocating fuel delivery.

mediaPlan.rationale: The fuel path is isolated on the model so the cluster gear, pump drive gear and coupling can be found.

steps.title: Oil and speed indication
steps.prompt: Trace the Oil and tachometer path. Section the pump housing and find the empty gear pockets. Follow the male spline into the cam-gear socket, then trace the pump driver and the 90-degree bevel pair to the lateral tach output.
steps.note: A-3-2; A-4-16 items 24/45/47; H C-3-2: tach output 0.5:1 CW facing its pad. The bevels are smooth pitch-form studies; teeth and spatial layout remain illustrative. The housing is placed left of the cam axis to clear the separate fuel bay. Figure A-4-8 items 10/11 are scavenge gears, not interchangeable tach labels. The IO-520 permold pump is a separate comparison study.

mediaPlan.rationale: The oil and tachometer path, with the sectioned pump housing and the bevel pair, is shown on the model.

steps.title: Electrical supply
steps.prompt: Select Alternator and explain the conversion from shaft power to aircraft electrical supply. Compare the marked remote endpoint with the documented shaft train.
steps.note: H C-3-3: 3:1 CW. A-4-13 supports the nested driven-gear cup, bushing, clutch sleeve and keyed hub represented here. Item 5 is the mounting gasket; the four-lug flange belongs to body item 4. The H photograph A-4-4 places the alternator toward the front; this module is relocated onto a grey teaching stand. These supports are not engine hardware. Rotor/stator and detailed clutch spring are omitted. The basic narrative mentions a generator pulley; its transfer geometry is not used as an H alternator claim. Dashed path is conceptual; transfer geometry remains unresolved.

mediaPlan.rationale: The alternator is selected on the model to follow the shaft train from the crankshaft.

steps.title: Optional aircraft loads
steps.prompt: Select the Vacuum path. Read the speed and viewpoint. Explain why a listed drive pad does not prove that a particular aircraft has the pump or that vacuum powers every aircraft instrument.
steps.note: A-3-2 describes optional upper-rear accessories through magneto gear splines. H C-3-3 lists vacuum, deice and autopilot drives at 1.14:1 CCW. Useful pneumatic function and equipment are installation dependent; exact adapter transfer geometry and accessory internals are omitted.

mediaPlan.rationale: The vacuum path is selected on the model to read its speed and viewpoint.

steps.title: Governor remote drive
steps.prompt: Select Governor. Trace crank → camshaft → front bevel drive → governor. Explain how mechanical speed sensing and oil control can change propeller blade angle.
steps.note: A-3-2 documents the front camshaft bevel pair. H C-3-3: 0.809:1 CW. Governor is a front remote output, relocated into this study; bevel shapes omitted. FAA PDF 27 and 294 explain blade-angle/speed and oil-control functions.

mediaPlan.rationale: The governor path is traced through the camshaft and the front bevel drive on the model.

steps.title: Why the propeller is geared down
steps.prompt:
Engines make more power by turning faster, but a propeller cannot follow. When the blade tips approach the speed of sound the propeller's efficiency falls rapidly.

Reduction gearing lets the engine run at a higher rpm and develop more power while the propeller turns slower, so its efficiency does not fall.

The GTSIO-520-H is geared. Its propeller drive ratio is 0.667:1, so the propeller turns at two-thirds of crankshaft speed. Its rating of 375 horsepower at 2,275 propeller rpm means the crankshaft runs at about 3,400 rpm (2,275 ÷ 0.667).

The gears carry the full engine torque, so they are machined from steel forgings.

Engines of low power turn the propeller directly: the propeller shaft is part of the crankshaft.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 44 (reduction gearing limits the propeller rotation speed; whenever the blade tips approach the speed of sound the propeller efficiency decreases rapidly; the engine runs at a higher rpm and develops more power while the propeller slows; gears machined from steel forgings; the propeller shaft of most low-power engines is forged as part of the crankshaft) and the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 152 (the -H: geared, 375 horsepower at 2275 propeller rpm, propeller drive ratio 0.667:1). The crankshaft speed of about 3,400 rpm is the quotient; the course deck quotes the same figures (slide 'Recap Discussion').

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: How a reduction gear is built
steps.prompt:
The figure shows three arrangements. In a spur planetary set, a sun gear splined to the crankshaft drives small planet gears on a carrier fixed to the propeller shaft, and the planets also mesh with a stationary bell gear. They roll round it and carry the propeller shaft in the same direction as the crankshaft, but slower. The bevel planetary set is more compact and suits a smaller step-down. The spur and pinion set suits lower-powered engines.

In the GTSIO-520-H, the splined front end of the crankshaft turns a quill shaft. The quill shaft turns a propeller shaft drive gear, and that drives the propeller shaft gear: a plain gear pair of the kind you tried in the explorer.
steps.alt: FAA diagram of propeller reduction gears: spur planetary, bevel planetary, and spur and pinion
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 44 (the three types most commonly used, spur planetary, bevel planetary, and spur and pinion; the spur planetary gearing: sun gear splined to the crankshaft, stationary bell gear, planetary pinions on a carrier ring fastened to the propeller shaft, the planets walking round the stationary gear so that the shaft turns in the crankshaft direction at a reduced speed; the bevel planetary type is more compact and used where a smaller step-down is desired; several lower-powered engines use the spur and pinion arrangement) and the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 17 (section A-3-2 a 4: the splined front end of the crankshaft transmits torque to the propeller shaft drive gear through an externally splined quill shaft, which drives the propeller shaft gear). The same figure is used in Parts and Construction.

mediaPlan.rationale: The FAA figure names the parts of the three reduction arrangements.

steps.title: Starting reverses power
steps.prompt: Before playing, predict the torque direction. Run Starter engagement and start. Pause during cranking, at engine takeover, and afterwards. Identify the [worm](StarterWorm), [worm wheel](WormWheel), [spring](ClutchSpring), [drum](StarterDrum) and [shaftgear](StarterShaftGear).
steps.note: A-3-2; A-4-15; FAA PDF 236 (5-6): spring tightens around drum during starting and releases after start. H starter drive 32:1 CCW facing pad applies during cranking. Clutch tightening, transition time and speed ramp are illustrative. No sliding Bendix pinion is added.

mediaPlan.rationale: The starter engagement clip is run on the model so the worm, worm wheel, spring, drum and shaftgear can be named at each stage.

steps.title: Engine takes over
steps.prompt: Scrub past the engine-takeover stage. Observe that [worm drive](StarterWorm) and [worm wheel](WormWheel) stop while the [shaftgear](StarterShaftGear) continues to turn with the crank gear. Explain why the clutch must separate these functions.
steps.note: A-3-2 supports clutch release and continued crank-driven shaftgear. Model times and motor stop are a staged illustration, not measured dynamics or an aircraft starting checklist.

mediaPlan.rationale: The model is scrubbed past engine takeover to see the worm drive stop while the shaftgear keeps turning.

steps.title: Reassemble relationships
steps.prompt: Reverse the exploded view. Pause halfway, isolate a complete path and inspect its seal and mounting interface. Return to assembled, then switch to normal operation and explain what must transmit torque.
steps.note: Manufacturer exploded figures support part relationships. This staged reassembly is pedagogical; fastener torques, clearances, service limits and actual maintenance sequence are not represented.

mediaPlan.rationale: Reversing the exploded view lets the learner isolate a complete path and inspect its seal and mounting interface.

steps.title: Wet sump and dry sump
steps.prompt:
The engine's oil must be stored somewhere. In a wet-sump system the oil is kept inside the engine, in the crankcase or the sump under it. One pump draws it from there and circulates it, and it drains back.

In a dry-sump system the oil is kept in an external tank. A scavenge pump pulls the oil out of the engine's shallow sump as it collects and returns it to the tank, and a pressure pump sends it back to the engine. Follow the loop in the picture: sump (1), scavenge pump (2), tank (3), pressure pump (4), and oil to the engine (5).

A dry-sump system has all the parts of a wet-sump one, plus the scavenge pump, tubing and tank.

The GTSIO-520-H holds its 13 quarts in a sump under the crankcase: a wet-sump engine.
steps.alt: Schematic of a dry-sump oil system: an engine block with a small sump at the bottom, a scavenge pump taking oil from the sump to an external oil tank, and a pressure pump returning oil from the tank to the engine, with numbered flow arrows.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 250 (the two basic classifications of reciprocating-engine lubrication: wet sump stores the oil in a reservoir inside the engine, returned to a crankcase-based reservoir; dry sump pumps the oil from the crankcase to an external tank, with a scavenge pump, external tubing and tank; the dry sump system contains all the components of the wet sump system) and the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 17 (the engine oil supply is contained in the sump; oil is drawn from the sump through the suction tube to the oil pump) and PDF p. 152 (oil sump capacity 13 quarts). Picture: 'Dry sump' by Arnero, in the public domain (Wikimedia Commons, File:Dry sump.svg; checked 13 October 2026); the numbers follow the legend of the English Wikipedia article Dry sump (1 sump, 2 scavenge pump, 3 oil tank, 4 pressure pump, 5 conditioned oil to the engine).

mediaPlan.rationale: A simple loop diagram shows where the oil is stored and which pump moves it where.

steps.title: When a drive fails
steps.prompt:
Each accessory depends on its drive. If the drive fails, the accessory stops. What follows depends on the accessory.

Magneto drive: that ignition system is lost. The other keeps firing its plugs, so the engine runs, with less efficient burning.

Oil pump drive: no oil pressure, and the engine is quickly damaged.

Fuel pump drive: engine-driven fuel flow stops.

Governor drive: propeller speed control is lost. Alternator drive: electrical output is lost. Vacuum or tachometer drive: suction or rpm indication is lost.

Some drives have a shear section, a deliberately weak shaft. If the pump seizes, that shaft breaks and the rest of the gear train is protected.
steps.note: The consequences are the lesson's reasoning from what each accessory does (see the earlier steps and FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 28, 84, 294 and 391). Dual ignition and its safety if one system fails: PDF p. 468 (glossary). The shear section that causes the shaft to shear if the pump gears seize, shown for a turbine engine's oil pump: PDF pp. 268 to 269. The course slides describe the same protection for a seized vacuum pump on piston engines ('Accessory Drive Failsafe Design', slides 'Accessory Gear Trains' and 'Recap Discussion'), which this step does not rely on alone: the GTSIO-520 manual pages read here do not describe it, so check the manual for the engine in front of you. Hypothetical reasoning, not an approved troubleshooting procedure.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Illustrative faults
steps.prompt: Discuss three hypothetical faults: (1) the fuel coupling transmits no torque, (2) the starter spring remains gripping after engine takeover, (3) a mounting seal leaks. For each, identify the first affected mechanical connection, its useful function and evidence needed before diagnosing the real engine.
steps.note: ILLUSTRATIVE FAULT SCENARIOS: hypothetical reasoning from A-3-2, A-4-11, A-4-15 and C-3-6; no measured wear, pressure, seizure, failure probability or approved troubleshooting procedure is simulated.

mediaPlan.rationale: A written reasoning prompt about hypothetical faults; the model and the earlier steps carry the evidence.

steps.title: Explain the complete path
steps.prompt:
Choose an accessory and give a short explanation: source of energy → gears → shaft or coupling → interface → useful function. State one verified ratio, its viewpoint and one model limitation.

Then say, in your own words: what a spur gear and a bevel gear are each for, why the propeller is geared down, how a wet sump differs from a dry sump, and what happens if a drive fails. Complete the knowledge checks.
steps.note: Verified endpoints are in H C-3-2/C-3-3. Unresolved fuel ratio and optional transfer geometry must remain unknown. This assembly does not borrow IO-520 permold configuration.

mediaPlan.rationale: The completion step asks the learner to explain in words.

lessons.title: Power Generation
lessons.objective: Follow the push from burning gas to the propeller shaft: explain why the spark comes before top dead centre, define compression ratio and calculate cylinder volumes, and recognise the order and the care needed to take the power section apart and put it back together.
lessons.purpose: Connect the entire energy-conversion chain from fuel to useful aircraft propulsion.
lessons.coreIdea: Chemical energy in fuel → combustion → thermal energy → pressure → piston force → reciprocating movement → crankshaft torque → shaft power → propeller power → thrust.
outcomes: Explain the sequence from chemical energy in fuel to thrust, one conversion at a time (see the core idea).
Explain that hydrocarbon fuel contains stored chemical energy.
Explain the role of fuel, air and ignition in releasing that energy through combustion.
Explain how combustion increases gas pressure and temperature inside the cylinder.
Explain how expanding gases exert force on the piston.
Explain how the connecting rod and crankshaft convert reciprocating motion into rotation.
Distinguish force, torque, rotational speed and shaft power.
Explain that the engine primarily produces shaft power while the propeller converts shaft power into thrust.
Explain how part of engine output is also consumed in driving engine accessories.
Recognise how engine mechanical power may indirectly support electrical, hydraulic and pneumatic aircraft services.
Identify the components forming the piston-engine power-generating assembly.
State the function of each major power-generation component.
Define compression ratio and explain its significance to engine operation.
Explain why combustion events must be correctly distributed among cylinders.
Define engine firing order.
Explain why multi-cylinder engines use an arranged firing sequence.
Explain how firing order contributes to smoother torque delivery, vibration control, cooling distribution and engine operation.
Relate firing order to cylinder numbering.
lessons.syllabusNote: The official module explicitly requires power-generation assembly components/functions and compression ratio. It also explicitly requires firing order.
lessons.completionCriteria: Follow the energy from the fuel to thrust one conversion at a time; explain what fuel, air and ignition each do; name the parts of the power-generating assembly and what each does; tell force, torque, rotational speed and shaft power apart and use torque and rpm to find power; explain why the spark fires before top dead centre and calculate the compression ratio and the swept and clearance volume of a cylinder; say how shaft power becomes thrust and where some of the power goes before the propeller; trace the push from the piston to the propeller shaft and state three things that must be kept in order when the power section is assembled; and explain why the power events are spread evenly around the cycle, what the firing order is and why it is not the numbering order.

steps.title: From fuel to thrust
steps.prompt:
The engine does not make power from nothing. It changes energy from one form to another, one conversion at a time, until the aircraft is pushed forward.

The fuel holds chemical energy, and burning turns it into heat. The heat raises the pressure of the gas in the cylinder. The pressure pushes on the piston, and the piston and connecting rod carry the push to the crankshaft. The crankshaft turns, so the push becomes torque, and torque at a speed is shaft power. The propeller turns shaft power into thrust.

The whole chain: fuel, heat, pressure, force, motion, torque, shaft power, propeller, thrust. Walk along it in the next step, then keep it in mind through the lesson.
steps.note: The chain is the lesson's core idea (the instructor's outcomes, objective 1). Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), glossary, PDF p. 472 (a heat engine converts the chemical energy in a fuel into heat energy and then into mechanical energy) and PDF pp. 46 to 48 and 52 to 54 (the burning gases push the piston down, the connecting rod movement is changed to rotary movement by the crankshaft and transmitted to the propeller shaft; torque and brake horsepower; thrust horsepower).

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Walk the energy chain
steps.prompt:
Step along the nine stages from fuel to thrust. At each one, say what form the energy has and what turns it into the next stage.

At the heat stage, look at where the heat goes. How much of it is used for power, and how much is lost?
steps.note: Schematic interactive made for this lesson. Every figure is the FAA handbook's, with its page: about 20,000 BTU per pound of fuel (PDF p. 55); 25 to 30 percent of the heat used for power output, 15 to 20 percent lost in cooling, 5 to 10 percent in friction and 40 to 45 percent through the exhaust (PDF p. 55); gas at 3,000 to 4,000 degrees F and a force greater than 15 tons on the piston (PDF p. 48); torque as force times distance (PDF p. 52); friction horsepower as much as 10 to 15 percent (PDF p. 53); an 85 percent efficient propeller turning 1,000 bhp into 850 thrust horsepower (PDF p. 54). The handbook gives the heat split as ranges, drawn as bands, and elsewhere (PDF p. 56) puts the thermal efficiency of a reciprocating engine at about 34 percent; real engines differ.

mediaPlan.rationale: Stepping along the chain, with the heat split drawn at the heat stage, makes each conversion and each loss visible in turn.

steps.title: Fuel, air and a spark
steps.prompt:
Fuel is the engine's stored energy. A pound of petroleum fuel, burned with enough air to consume it completely, gives up about 20,000 BTU: the equivalent of 15,560,000 ft-lb of mechanical work. That chemical energy stays locked in the fuel until it burns.

Burning needs three things together. The fuel supplies the energy. The air supplies the oxygen the fuel burns in. The ignition starts the burn at the right moment: in this engine the spark plugs fire as the piston approaches TDC.

Take any one away and no energy is released. Too little air, or a weak or badly timed spark, and the burn is poor and the energy is wasted. How much fuel for how much air is the mixture, which lesson 13 explains.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 55 (a pound of petroleum fuel, burned with enough air to consume it completely, gives up about 20,000 BTU, the equivalent of 15,560,000 ft-lb of mechanical work) and PDF p. 48 (the charge is fired by an electric spark as the piston approaches TDC). The three requirements for burning (fuel, air for its oxygen, and ignition) are the lesson's explanation of the handbook's account of the four events.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Burning gas pushes the piston
steps.prompt:
Burning raises the temperature and pressure of the gas trapped in the cylinder. Both valves are shut, so the gas cannot escape, and it reaches between 3,000 and 4,000 °F.

That pressure pushes on the piston crown. Force is pressure times area, and at full power the push can be more than 15 tons.

Everything the engine does for the aircraft starts with this push. Before you open the model, predict the path: what carries the push from the piston to the propeller, and what has to be strong enough to survive it?
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48 (the piston is pushed down by the burning gases with a force that can be greater than 15 tons at maximum power; the gas temperature may be between 3,000 and 4,000 °F; the connecting rod movement is changed to rotary movement by the crankshaft and transmitted to the propeller shaft) and PDF p. 51 (the area of the piston multiplied by the pressure gives the force acting on the piston in pounds). The handbook writes the force as "(30,000 psi)"; 15 tons is about 30,000 pounds of force, so the lesson gives the force and not a pressure. That both valves are closed during the power stroke: Figure 1-36, PDF p. 47.

mediaPlan.rationale: A prediction prompt frames the model step that follows.

steps.title: Spark before TDC
steps.prompt: At 340° of the cycle [the piston](PistonBody) is still rising towards top dead centre, 20° before it gets there. The spark fires about now. Burning takes time, so the charge is lit early enough that it has burned completely when the piston is just past TDC and ready to be pushed down. Why would it be wrong to treat this pose as the timing for every engine?
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48: the charge is fired as the piston approaches TDC, the time of ignition varies from 20° to 35° before TDC depending on the engine, to ensure complete combustion by the time the piston is slightly past TDC, and the ignition system must be timed to the manufacturer's recommendations. The GTSIO-520 overhaul manual lists spark at 20° BTC for both magnetos (PDF p. 153, C-3-3). The 340° pose is that figure placed on the model's ideal profile; the model is not timing data. The cylinder is a teaching reconstruction of the GTSIO-520-H cylinder (reviewed release): part shapes and the motions are illustrative.

mediaPlan.rationale: The shared 720-degree cylinder profile puts the learner 20 degrees before TDC on the compression stroke.

steps.title: Compression ratio
steps.prompt: The compression ratio compares the volume in the cylinder with the piston at the bottom of its stroke to the volume with the piston at the top. In the figure the total volume at the bottom is seven times the clearance volume left at the top, so the ratio is 7 to 1, written 7:1. Squeezing the charge more makes it able to do more work, like squeezing a spring, but the ratio is limited by the fuel grades, the engine speeds and the manifold pressures an engine must use.
steps.alt: FAA drawing of two cylinders side by side: at bottom dead centre the whole cylinder is filled and marked in seven equal slices, and at top dead centre only the clearance volume, one slice, remains. Total volume, displacement volume and clearance volume are marked.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 50-51 (the compression ratio compares the volume of space in a cylinder with the piston at the bottom of the stroke to the volume with the piston at the top; 140 cubic inches to 20 cubic inches is 7:1; it is limited by present-day fuel grades, engine speeds and manifold pressures; Figure 1-38).

mediaPlan.rationale: The figure shows total, displacement and clearance volume on one drawing.

steps.title: Swept and clearance volume
steps.prompt: Move the crank and switch between the swept volume, the clearance volume and the total volume. The clearance volume is what is left above the piston at TDC, and the swept volume is the volume the piston sweeps in one stroke. Check that the total volume divided by the clearance volume gives the compression ratio drawn.
steps.note: Schematic interactive from the Terminologies lesson. It draws the GTSIO-520-H compression ratio of 7.5:1 (overhaul manual, Chapter C-3, PDF p. 152) with a constant bore, so heights are proportional to volumes. It is not a to-scale drawing of the combustion chamber.

mediaPlan.rationale: Switching between swept, clearance and total volume makes the ratio something the learner can see.

steps.title: Worked example: one cylinder
steps.prompt: Take the GTSIO-520-H: bore 5.250 in, stroke 4.000 in, compression ratio 7.5:1. The swept volume (piston displacement) of one cylinder is 0.7854 × 5.25² × 4.00 = 86.6 cu in. Six cylinders give 519.5, which the manual rounds to 520 cu in. The clearance volume follows from the ratio: total volume ÷ clearance volume = 7.5, and total volume = swept + clearance, so clearance = swept ÷ (7.5 − 1) = 86.6 ÷ 6.5 = 13.3 cu in. The total volume is 86.6 + 13.3 = 99.9 cu in. Check that 99.9 ÷ 13.3 is 7.5.
steps.note: Calculation from the bore, stroke and compression ratio in the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 152 (C-3-2: bore 5.250 in, stroke 4.000 in, displacement 520 cu in, compression ratio 7.5:1) using the piston displacement method in FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 49-50 (area of the base × stroke; × number of cylinders). The course deck (slide 212) works the same example.

mediaPlan.rationale: A worked calculation reads best as text the learner can redo.

steps.title: High compression and fuel
steps.prompt: A higher compression ratio, and a higher manifold pressure, raise the pressure of the charge just before the spark. If it gets too high, one of two things happens. In pre-ignition the charge starts to burn before the spark plug fires. In detonation the spark plug lights the charge, but instead of burning at a controlled rate it explodes, and the cylinder temperature and pressure spike. Left for long enough either can damage or destroy the engine. High-compression engines therefore use high-octane fuel, and some limit their maximum manifold pressure. The GTSIO-520-H calls for 100LL or 100 grade fuel.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 50 (compression ratio and manifold pressure determine the cylinder pressure before ignition; pre-ignition and detonation defined; high-octane fuel and limiting manifold pressure) and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 152 (fuel, aviation grade, 100LL blue or 100 green). The handbook's simple rule that the pressure before ignition is the manifold pressure times the compression ratio ignores that compression heats the gas, so this step gives no number. Backfiring, detonation and pre-ignition are covered again in the Operation Malfunctions lesson.

mediaPlan.rationale: A cause-and-effect step that sets up the malfunctions lesson.

steps.title: From piston to crankshaft
steps.prompt: Now follow the push. At 400° the piston is on its power stroke. The gas presses on the [piston crown](PistonBody), the piston pushes through the [piston pin](FloatingPin) to the [connecting rod](ConnectingRodBody), and the rod, which changes its angle as it goes, pushes on the [crankpin](CrankThrow). The crankpin is off the centre of the crankshaft, so the push turns it. The rotation goes on to the propeller shaft. Which of these parts slide, and which turn?
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48 (the piston is forced down by the burning gases; the downward movement of the connecting rod is changed to rotary movement by the crankshaft, which transmits it to the propeller shaft). The one-cylinder model shows a single crank throw. The cylinder is a teaching reconstruction of the GTSIO-520-H cylinder (reviewed release): part shapes and the motions are illustrative.

mediaPlan.rationale: The spotlit parts show the force path from the piston crown to the crankpin.

steps.title: The power-generating assembly
steps.prompt:
The parts that turn burning gas into rotation form the power-generating assembly.

The cylinder holds the burning gas, and its head carries the valves and spark plugs. The piston takes the push of the gas, and its rings seal the gas in and control the oil. The piston pin joins the piston to the connecting rod, and the rod carries the push to the crankpin. The crankshaft changes the back-and-forth motion into rotation and passes it to the propeller shaft. The crankcase holds the crankshaft in its main bearings, and the cylinders are fastened to it.

The valves, and the cams that work them, let the gas in and out at the right moments (lesson 8).

Name them on the model. Which part receives the push, and which part turns?
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 26 (the basic major components of a reciprocating engine: crankcase, cylinders, pistons, connecting rods, valves and valve-operating mechanism, and crankshaft), PDF pp. 28 to 30 (the crankshaft transforms the reciprocating motion of the piston and connecting rod into rotary motion; the connecting rod) and PDF p. 48. The functions are those of Parts and Construction, where each part is taken in turn.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Piston rings and ring gaps
steps.prompt: The rings seal the gas above the piston and control the oil on the cylinder wall. Each ring is split, so it has a gap. When a piston is assembled the gaps are not lined up: on the GTSIO-520 pistons the first, third and fifth ring gaps go one side of the piston and the second and fourth go on the opposite side, 180° away. With the gaps staggered, gas that gets past one ring meets a solid part of the next. If the gaps line up, a straight path opens for gas to leak past the piston into the crankcase and for oil to be burned.
steps.note: Documented from the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 75 (11-8: five-ring pistons have the first, third and fifth gaps toward the top of the piston and the second and fourth 180° apart from them; four-ring pistons have the first and third gaps on top and the second and fourth 180° away; do not intermix piston types in any one engine). The reason for staggering (less blow-by and oil burning) is from the course deck (slides 168-169) and the daily quiz; the manual gives the positions.

mediaPlan.rationale: The positions are a rule in the manual and read best as text.

steps.title: Taking the power section apart
steps.prompt: The manual removes a cylinder in a set order. Position the crankshaft so the valve lifters of the cylinder are on the heels (base circles) of their cam lobes and both valves are fully closed, then take off the rocker covers, rocker assemblies and pushrods. Make sure the piston is at top dead centre, take off the base nuts, and draw the cylinder straight out, catching the piston as it clears the barrel so it does not fall. Support the cylinder on a block when you remove its valve springs, and stone down any nicks on the valve stems before the valves come out. Parts that came off together stay together.
steps.note: Documented from the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF pp. 57-58 (7-15: lifters on the heels of the cam lobes with both valves closed; rocker assemblies and pushrods removed; piston at top dead centre; cylinder withdrawn straight outward and the piston caught; a wood block to hold the cylinder while the valve springs are removed; stone down nicks before removing the valves; exhaust valves, rotocaps and hydraulic lifters recommended for replacement). This is a recognition lesson, not a procedure: follow the manual itself, including its cautions, for any real work.

mediaPlan.rationale: A sequence with reasons; the manual is the procedure and the lesson shows why it is in that order.

steps.title: Putting it back together
steps.prompt: Assembly follows the same care in reverse. Connecting rods go on with their position numbers up, odd-numbered rods extended to the right and even-numbered to the left, and their nuts are torqued to specification and safetied. Rotate the crankshaft to put the rod in its outermost position, then fit the piston with the position number on its head facing forward. Check the ring gaps, compress the rings with a ring compressor and slide the cylinder on. Fit cylinders 4 and 5 first, then 2 and 3, then 1 and 6, so the crankshaft is turned as little as possible and stays balanced. Tighten the base nuts in the manual's sequence to the value in its Chapter B.
steps.note: Documented from the Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF pp. 75-76 (11-10: rods laid out by the position number stamped on the bolt bosses, position numbers on top, odd-numbered rods to the right; nuts torqued and safetied with cotter pins) and PDF pp. 79-80 (12-3: crankshaft turned so the rod is outermost; the position number on the piston head forward; the ring compressor; install Nos. 4 and 5 first, then 2 and 3, then 1 and 6; torque in the sequence of Figure A4-38 to the value in Chapter B). This is a recognition lesson, not a procedure.

mediaPlan.rationale: The assembly rules and their reasons read best as text.

steps.title: Force, torque, speed and power
steps.prompt:
Four words are easy to mix up.

Force is a push or pull, in pounds. Gas pressure times piston area gives the force on a piston.

Torque is a force turning something: the force times its distance from the axis, at right angles to the force. It is measured in pound-feet. A push of 200 lb on an arm 3.18 ft long gives 636 lb-ft.

Rotational speed is how fast the shaft turns, in rpm.

Power is the rate of doing work. Torque and speed together make shaft power: bhp = 2π × torque × rpm ÷ 33,000, with torque in lb-ft. That torque at 3,000 rpm is 363 hp.

The same power can be a high torque at a low speed or a low torque at a high speed.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 51 (the area of the piston multiplied by the pressure gives the force acting on the piston in pounds), PDF p. 49 (work is force times distance; one horsepower is 33,000 ft-lb per minute) and PDF pp. 52 to 53 (torque is the product of a force and the distance of the force from the axis about which it acts, in lb-ft; a Prony brake with a 200 lb scale reading on a 3.18 ft arm gives 636 lb-ft; work per revolution is 2π times the torque; bhp = 2π × force × arm × rpm ÷ 33,000, 363 hp at 3,000 rpm; horsepower is a function of both torque and rpm).

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Shaft power to thrust
steps.prompt:
The piston engine's output is shaft power, rated in brake horsepower. It does not make thrust itself. The propeller does, by turning shaft power into thrust.
