The useful output of every aircraft powerplant is thrust, the force that propels the aircraft. Since the piston engine is rated in brake horsepower, the useful output of engine and propeller together is measured as thrust horsepower.

The propeller is never 100 percent efficient, and its efficiency varies with engine speed, altitude, temperature and airspeed. With a propeller of 85 percent efficiency, an engine of 1,000 bhp gives 850 thrust horsepower.

Of the horsepowers the handbook discusses, thrust horsepower decides the performance of the engine and propeller together.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 23 (the useful output of all aircraft powerplants is thrust, the force which propels the aircraft; the reciprocating engine is rated in brake horsepower) and PDF p. 54 (thrust horsepower is the result of the engine and propeller working together; the efficiency of the propeller varies with engine speed, attitude, altitude, temperature and airspeed; an engine developing 1,000 bhp with an 85 percent efficient propeller gives 850 thrust hp; of the four types of horsepower, thrust horsepower determines the performance of the engine-propeller combination).

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Power the engine keeps for itself
steps.prompt:
Not all the power the burning gas makes reaches the propeller. The power developed in the cylinders is the indicated horsepower. Part of it, the friction horsepower, goes in overcoming friction, drawing in fuel, expelling exhaust, and driving the oil and fuel pumps and other accessories: as much as 10 to 15 percent in modern aircraft engines. What is left at the propeller shaft is the brake horsepower.

Some accessory power goes on to serve the aircraft. The alternator or generator supplies the electrical system. A vacuum pump supplies suction, which is a pneumatic service. On aircraft with a hydraulic system an engine-driven pump supplies it. The GTSIO-520-H lists vacuum, de-icing and autopilot drives as options.

These services take engine power indirectly: the engine turns the accessory, and the accessory serves the aircraft.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 52 to 53 (the power delivered to the propeller is brake horsepower; friction horsepower is the indicated minus the brake horsepower and is the power used in overcoming the friction of moving parts, drawing in fuel, expelling exhaust, driving oil and fuel pumps and other engine accessories; on modern aircraft engines the loss may be as high as 10 to 15 percent of the indicated horsepower) and Figure 1-41 (PDF p. 55), which draws accessories as part of the friction power. Generator, vacuum pump and starter on the accessory section: PDF p. 28. The vacuum, de-icing and autopilot drives listed as options: GTSIO-520 reviewed manual, H section C-3-3. The engine-driven hydraulic pump is from the course slides (hydraulic pumps among the accessories driven through spur gears) and general practice, not from the manual pages read here: check the aircraft's own documents.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Why spread the power events
steps.prompt:
One cylinder gets a power stroke once in every two turns of the crankshaft. If every cylinder fired at the same moment, the shaft would get one hard push every two turns and nothing in between.

So the power events are spread over the 720° of the cycle. Divide 720° by the number of cylinders: a four-cylinder engine has a power event every 180° of crankshaft rotation, a six-cylinder engine every 120°, and a nine-cylinder radial every 80°.

Even spacing gives steadier torque and less vibration. It also spreads the heat and the loads in time, instead of piling them into one moment. That is why the combustion events must be correctly distributed among the cylinders.
steps.note: The four-stroke cycle takes 720 degrees of crankshaft rotation: FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 46. The spacing (720 divided by the number of cylinders) is arithmetic, and the nine-cylinder figure of 80 degrees is in the course slides (slide 'Firing Order - Radial') and in the handbook's spacing of 40 degrees between cylinders with 80 degrees between firing impulses (PDF p. 40). The handbook says the firing order is designed to provide for balance and to eliminate vibration to the greatest extent possible (PDF p. 37). Steadier torque and the spreading of heat and loads: the course slides (slide 'Firing Order': reduce vibration, ensure smooth power delivery, optimize engine cooling, prevent mechanical stress), which the handbook pages read here do not state in these words. The course slide 'Firing Order - H.O.' gives the interval as 120 degrees for four cylinders and 60 degrees for six; the arithmetic gives 180 and 120, and this lesson follows the arithmetic.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Firing order and a smooth engine
steps.prompt:
The firing order is the sequence in which the power events occur in the cylinders. It is not simply 1, 2, 3, 4, because neighbouring cylinders firing one after another would load one part of the engine and one part of the crankshaft at a time.

The order is designed to give balance and to eliminate vibration as far as possible. In inline engines the firing is spread evenly along the crankshaft. In opposed engines the order can be listed in pairs, because each pair fires across the centre main bearing.

On a six-cylinder opposed engine the order 1-4-5-2-3-6 alternates between the two banks. A four-cylinder one is 1-3-2-4 on the Lycoming O-360, though another model is 1-4-2-3.

A good order also helps the cooling, since the heat is not added to the same part twice in a row.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 37 (the firing order is the sequence in which the power event occurs in the different cylinders; designed to provide for balance and to eliminate vibration to the greatest extent possible; in inline engines, evenly distributed along the crankshaft; in opposed engines listed in pairs, as each pair fires across the center main bearing; six-cylinder opposed 1-4-5-2-3-6; one four-cylinder model 1-4-2-3 and another 1-3-2-4) and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF p. 153 (the -H: 1-4-5-2-3-6). The O-360 as 1-3-2-4: course slides (slide 'Firing Order - H.O.'). The benefit to cooling is from the course slides only (slide 'Firing Order'); the sentence on alternating banks is read from the order itself, with odd cylinders on the right and even on the left.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Firing order is not numbering order
steps.prompt:
Firing order and cylinder numbering are different things. The numbers only name the cylinders. On the GTSIO-520-H they run from the rear, odd on the right and even on the left, as seen from the accessory end. The firing order says in what sequence the named cylinders fire.

Read a firing order as a list of names. In 1-4-5-2-3-6, No. 1 fires, then No. 4, then No. 5. After No. 6 the sequence starts again with No. 1.

Makers number differently. Lycoming has No. 1 on the right side closest to the propeller; Continental has it at the right rear. A six-cylinder Lycoming is typically 1-4-5-2-3-6 and a Continental normally 1-6-3-2-5-4, though this engine's manual gives 1-4-5-2-3-6.

So use the manual for the engine in front of you.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 36 (the numbering of opposed engine cylinders is by no means standard; some manufacturers number from the rear and others from the front; refer to the engine manual), the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual (PDF pp. 13 to 14: cylinders numbered from the rear, odd on the right and even on the left, as seen from the accessory end; PDF p. 153: the -H firing order 1-4-5-2-3-6) and EASA Module 16 core text, PDF p. 12 (Lycoming and Continental firing orders and numbering systems). The Continental order 1-6-3-2-5-4 is the one in the IO-520 manual; the GTSIO-520-H manual lists a different order, as the Classification lesson shows.

mediaPlan.rationale: Words carry this step; a picture would add nothing the sentences do not say.

steps.title: Name the whole path
steps.prompt:
Explain the whole story in your own words. How does the energy in the fuel become thrust, one conversion at a time? How do the spark timing, the compression ratio and the fuel work together to make the push, and how does the push reach the propeller shaft?

How do torque and speed make power, and where does some of the power go before the propeller? Why do the cylinders fire in a sequence, and is that the same as the numbering?

Then take the lesson's quiz.
steps.note: Completion step: the learner pulls the lesson together (opening prompt, action, feedback, completion evidence) from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 36 to 37 and 46 to 55, and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF pp. 57 to 58, 75 to 76, 79 to 80 and 153.

mediaPlan.rationale: The learner explains the whole path in their own words.

checks.question: Put these parts in the order the motion passes through them, from the cam to the valve.
checks.hint: The motion starts where the cam pushes and ends where the valve opens.
checks.rationale: The lobe lifts the tappet, the tappet moves the pushrod, the pushrod tips the rocker arm, and the rocker arm presses the valve open.

checks.question: The crankshaft of a four-stroke engine turns at 2,700 rpm. How fast does the camshaft turn?
checks.hint: A four-stroke cycle takes two turns of the crankshaft, and each valve opens once per cycle.
checks.rationale: The camshaft turns once for every two turns of the crankshaft, so it runs at half the speed: 2,700 ÷ 2 = 1,350 rpm. Its gear is twice the size of the crankshaft gear.

checks.question: What decides how far a valve lifts and how long it stays open?
checks.hint: Think about the part that does the pushing.
answers: The shape of the cam lobe
The strength of the valve spring
The length of the pushrod housing
The oil pressure in the tappet
checks.rationale: Valve lift and valve duration are both set by the shape of the cam lobe: a taller lobe lifts the valve further and a wider lobe holds it open longer.

checks.question: Why can an intake valve be made of a different steel from an exhaust valve?
checks.hint: One of them sits in the stream of burned gas.
answers: It runs cooler, so it does not need the most heat-resistant steel
It carries a heavier spring load
It is always hollow and filled with sodium
checks.rationale: Intake valves operate at lower temperatures, so chromic-nickel steel will do. Exhaust valves run hotter and use nichrome, silchrome or cobalt-chromium steel, which resist heat much better.

checks.question: What does the sodium inside a hollow valve stem do?
checks.hint: Sodium melts at about 208 °F and moves as the valve moves.
answers: It carries heat from the valve head up the stem to the guide
It lubricates the valve guide
It adds weight so the valve closes faster
checks.rationale: The liquid sodium is sloshed up and down by the valve motion and carries heat away from the head, which can cool the valve by 300 to 400 °F. Never cut open or scrap a sodium valve as ordinary metal: sodium exposed to air or water burns or explodes.

checks.question: Match each valve-train part to its job.
checks.hint: Use the cylinder model from the lesson.

pairs.right: Keeps the stem square to the seat as it slides
Lock the springs to the groove in the stem
Pivots on its shaft to turn pushrod lift into valve opening
Gives the valve face a hard surface to close on

checks.rationale: The guide keeps the stem aligned, the retainer and split keepers hold the springs on the stem, the rocker arm reverses the direction of the pushrod’s lift, and the seat insert is the durable surface the valve face seals against.

checks.question: Match each engine layout to the way its valves are worked.
checks.hint: One has a camshaft and one has a ring.

pairs.right: A camshaft in the crankcase, turning at half crankshaft speed
A cam ring around the crankshaft, with an intake track and an exhaust track

checks.rationale: An opposed engine has a camshaft in the crankcase that always turns at half crankshaft speed. A radial engine has a cam ring concentric with the crankshaft, with one track of lobes for the intake valves and one for the exhaust valves.

checks.question: What does a hydraulic tappet do that a solid tappet cannot?
checks.hint: Think about the gap in the valve train.
answers: It keeps the valve clearance at zero without any adjustment
It makes the valve stay open for longer
It lets the camshaft turn faster than the crankshaft
checks.rationale: Oil trapped under the plunger takes up the clearance automatically and follows the expansion and contraction of the valve train, so no clearance adjustment mechanism is needed.

checks.question: On an engine with solid tappets, what can wrong valve clearance change?
checks.hint: It changes when the valves really open and close.
answers: The valve overlap, and with it the idle mixture
The firing order of the cylinders
The direction the camshaft turns
checks.rationale: Too much clearance shortens the overlap and too little lengthens it. That changes how much gas is drawn back into the cylinder at idle, so the mixture changes, and it changes by a different amount in each cylinder.

checks.question: A valve has been ground until its edge is very thin, a feather edge. What can that cause?
checks.hint: A thin edge cannot lose its heat.
answers: Pre-ignition, because the thin edge overheats and burns away
Low oil pressure in the rocker box
A cracked valve spring
checks.rationale: A feather edge overheats, can cause pre-ignition and burns away in a short time. After re-facing, the edge must not be thinner than the manufacturer’s limit.

checks.question: An inner valve spring (P/N 637836) is compressed to 1.329 in. The tester reads 70 lb. The manual gives a serviceable limit of 73 lb at that height. What do you conclude?
checks.hint: Compare the reading with the serviceable limit.
answers: The spring is weaker than the serviceable limit and is not reused
The spring is serviceable because it is above 60 lb
The spring is a new part because it is below 78 lb
checks.rationale: A spring must push back with at least the serviceable limit at the test height. 70 lb is below 73 lb, so it is not reused. A new inner spring gives 78 to 88 lb at that height.

checks.question: During which two strokes are both valves closed?
checks.hint: Gas has to be trapped to be squeezed and then burned.
answers: Compression and power
Intake and exhaust
Intake and compression
Power and exhaust
checks.rationale: Both valves stay on their seats for the compression stroke and the power stroke, which seals the cylinder. The intake valve is open for the intake stroke and the exhaust valve for the exhaust stroke, and both are open together for a short while in the overlap.

checks.question: Match each timing term to its meaning.
checks.hint: Lead is early. Lag is late.

pairs.right: A valve opens before the piston reaches the end of its stroke
A valve closes after the piston has passed the end of its stroke
Both valves are off their seats at once around TDC
How long a valve is held open, set by the shape of the cam lobe

checks.rationale: Lead opens a valve early, lag closes it late, and overlap is the interval around TDC when the intake valve has opened and the exhaust valve has not yet closed. Duration is set by the cam lobe, as the lift is.

checks.question: Why does the exhaust valve start to open before BDC, while the cylinder still holds pressure?
checks.hint: What is left in the cylinder that can push the gas out?
answers: The pressure left in the cylinder pushes the gas out quickly and frees the cylinder of waste heat
It lets fresh mixture in sooner
It raises the compression ratio
The cam lobe is worn and opens it too early
checks.rationale: The valve opens considerably before BDC so that the remaining pressure forces the gas out as soon as possible. That frees the cylinder of waste heat and avoids overheating the cylinder and the piston.

checks.question: Why is the intake valve held open for a while after BDC?
checks.hint: Think of gas already moving through the intake pipe.
answers: The incoming charge has momentum and keeps filling the cylinder while the piston starts to rise
It lets the burned gas escape
It lowers the compression ratio
It reduces the valve lift
checks.rationale: Near BDC the piston moves very little, so the moving charge keeps flowing in and fills the cylinder more completely. Close it too late and the gas is forced back out through the intake valve.

checks.question: What is lined up when the camshaft gear is meshed with the crankshaft gear?
checks.hint: Each gear carries a mark for this job.
answers: The timing marks on the two gears
The spark plug gaps
The oil holes in the pushrods
The fins of the cylinders
checks.rationale: Meshing the gears with their timing marks aligned sets the camshaft to the crankshaft, so each lobe lifts its valve at the right crank angle.

checks.question: A valve timing chart shows the intake valve opening 20° before TDC and closing 60° after BDC. For how many degrees of crank angle is it open?
checks.hint: Add the angle before TDC, the 180° of the intake stroke and the angle after BDC.
checks.rationale: The valve is open for 20° before TDC, then through the whole 180° intake stroke, then 60° after BDC: 20 + 180 + 60 = 260°.

checks.question: The intake valve opens 35° before TDC and the exhaust valve closes 20° after TDC. How many degrees of valve overlap is that?
checks.hint: Overlap runs from the intake valve opening to the exhaust valve closing, across TDC.
checks.rationale: Both valves are open from 35° before TDC to 20° after it: 35 + 20 = 55°.

checks.question: A radial engine's cam ring has four lobes on each track. The crankshaft turns at 2,000 rpm. How fast does the ring turn?
checks.hint: Each valve opens once in two crankshaft turns, and each ring lobe opens it once per ring turn. The ring speed is the crankshaft speed divided by twice the number of lobes.
checks.rationale: Ring speed = crankshaft speed ÷ (2 × lobes) = 2,000 ÷ (2 × 4) = 250 rpm, one eighth of crankshaft speed, as in the handbook table.

checks.question: Why does a radial engine use a cam ring and not a straight camshaft?
checks.hint: Think about where the cylinders of a radial are.
answers: The cylinders spread around the crankshaft, and a ring around the crankshaft is the same distance from every cylinder
A ring makes the valves open twice as often
A radial engine has no valves to operate
A ring needs no gear to drive it
checks.rationale: The cylinders of a radial are arranged around the crankshaft, so a ring concentric with the crankshaft can work the tappet of every cylinder through its pushrod. The ring is driven by the crankshaft through gearing, at a much lower speed.

checks.question: Tap a pushrod housing.
checks.hint: It is the tube that carries each pushrod from the crankcase up to the cylinder head.
checks.rationale: The pushrod runs inside its housing, a tube between the crankcase and the cylinder head. The housing also returns oil from the rocker arm to the crankcase.

checks.question: Tap the camshaft and its drive.
checks.hint: It lies inside the crankcase and is turned by a gear from the crankshaft.
checks.rationale: The camshaft lies in the crankcase, driven at half crankshaft speed by a gear that meshes with the crankshaft gear. Its lobes lift the tappets.

checks.question: Name the highlighted part.
checks.hint: It is small and sits right at the tip of the valve stem.
answers: Valve keepers (split keys)
Spring retainer
Valve guide
Valve seat insert
checks.rationale: These are the keepers: tapered half-rounds that fit a groove cut near the tip of the stem and lock the spring retainer to it. Without them the springs could not hold the valve on its seat.

checks.question: Name the highlighted part.
checks.hint: The valve stem slides inside it.
answers: Valve guide
Valve seat insert
Pushrod housing
Rocker shaft
checks.rationale: This is the valve guide. The stem slides in it, and it keeps the valve square to its seat, so the face closes evenly every time.

checks.question: Name the highlighted part.
checks.hint: It runs from the tappet up to the rocker arm.
answers: Pushrod
Pushrod housing
Rocker shaft
Valve stem
checks.rationale: This is the pushrod. The tappet lifts it and it tips the rocker arm. It is hollow, and engine oil reaches the rocker arm through it; the housing around it is the tube that returns the oil.

checks.question: Name the highlighted part on the exhaust valve.
checks.hint: The springs push up against it.
answers: Spring retainer (Rotocoil type)
Valve keepers (split keys)
Inner valve spring
Rocker arm
checks.rationale: This is the spring retainer. The springs sit under it and it is locked to the stem by the keepers. On the exhaust valve this engine uses a Rotocoil type of retainer.

checks.question: Match each accessory to its job.
checks.hint: Think about what the aircraft or the engine would lose without it.

pairs.right: Makes the spark for the spark plugs
Pushes oil to the bearings under pressure
Turns the tachometer that shows crankshaft rpm
Spins the propeller governor that holds propeller speed
Makes electricity for the aircraft

checks.rationale: The magnetos make the spark, the oil pump keeps the bearings supplied with pressurised oil, the tachometer drive shows crankshaft rpm, the governor drive lets the governor hold propeller speed by changing blade angle with oil, and the alternator supplies the aircraft electrical system.

checks.question: Which path drives the GTSIO-520 magnetos?
checks.hint: Start at the crankshaft gear and follow the gears in order.
answers: Crankshaft gear → idler gear → the two magneto drive gears
Camshaft cluster gear → fuel coupling → magnetos
Propeller flange → starter motor → magnetos
checks.rationale: In the manual the crankshaft gear drives the idler gear, and the idler gear drives the magneto drive gears. The fuel pump and the oil pump are driven from the camshaft gear instead.

checks.question: The GTSIO-520-H magneto drive ratio to the crankshaft is 1.5:1. The crankshaft turns at 2,000 rpm. How fast does a magneto drive shaft turn?
checks.hint: Multiply the crankshaft speed by the ratio.
checks.rationale: The drive turns 1.5 times for every crankshaft turn: 1.5 × 2,000 = 3,000 rpm. This is the speed of the drive shaft, not a count of sparks.

checks.question: The H accessory table states a drive turns clockwise facing the engine drive pad. From the opposite end it appears:
checks.hint: Imagine walking round to the other side of the shaft.
answers: Counterclockwise
Clockwise
Stopped
checks.rationale: Apparent rotation reverses with the viewpoint, so the table states the viewpoint. The actual rotation has not changed.

checks.question: A 14-tooth gear drives a 28-tooth gear. The driver turns at 2,400 rpm. How fast does the 28-tooth gear turn?
checks.hint: The driven speed is the driver speed times driver teeth over driven teeth.
checks.rationale: Speed ratio = 14 ÷ 28 = 0.5, so the big gear turns at half speed: 2,400 × 0.5 = 1,200 rpm.

checks.question: A 12-tooth driver turns at 3,000 rpm and must drive a gear at 1,000 rpm. How many teeth must the driven gear have?
checks.hint: The speed ratio is 1,000 ÷ 3,000. Driver teeth ÷ driven teeth equals that ratio.
checks.rationale: The speed ratio is 1,000 ÷ 3,000 = 1/3, so the driven gear needs three times the driver's teeth: 12 × 3 = 36.

checks.question: An idler gear is put between a driver and a driven gear. What does it do?
checks.hint: Count the meshes. Each one reverses the direction.
answers: It makes the driven gear turn the same way as the driver and leaves the speed ratio unchanged
It doubles the speed of the driven gear
It makes the driven gear turn slower than the ratio of the teeth says
It stops the driven gear turning
checks.rationale: Each mesh reverses the direction, so two meshes give the driver's direction again. The speed ratio depends only on the driver and driven teeth, so the idler does not change it.

checks.question: Match each gear type to its use.
checks.hint: Think about the angle between the shafts.

pairs.right: Parallel shafts; heavier loaded drives and those needing least backlash
Shafts meeting at an angle, such as the stub shafts to angled accessory pads
A sun gear, planet gears on a carrier and a stationary ring that slow the propeller

checks.rationale: Spur gears serve parallel shafts, and the handbook gives them the heavier loaded accessories and those that need the least backlash. Bevel gears let a drive turn through an angle. A planetary set is one way to build a propeller reduction gear.

checks.question: Why do some powerful engines drive the propeller through reduction gears?
checks.hint: Think about what happens to a propeller whose blade tips approach the speed of sound.
answers: The engine can run fast to make more power while the propeller turns slower and stays efficient
The gears make the propeller turn faster than the crankshaft
The gears remove the need for a propeller governor
Direct drive is not allowed on large engines
checks.rationale: Blade tips approaching the speed of sound lose efficiency rapidly. Reduction gearing lets the engine run at a higher rpm for more power while the propeller turns at a speed at which it works efficiently.

checks.question: A geared engine has a propeller drive ratio of 0.667:1. The crankshaft turns at 3,000 rpm. How fast does the propeller turn?
checks.hint: Multiply the crankshaft speed by the drive ratio.
checks.rationale: 0.667 × 3,000 = 2,001 rpm: the propeller turns at about two-thirds of crankshaft speed.

checks.question: Match each term to its meaning in an oil system.
checks.hint: One system keeps its oil inside the engine and one keeps it in a tank outside.

pairs.right: Oil is stored inside the engine, in the crankcase or the sump under it
Oil is stored in an external tank
Returns oil from the engine to the tank
Sends oil to the engine's bearings

checks.rationale: A wet-sump engine stores its oil inside itself; a dry-sump engine carries the oil in a tank. The dry-sump system needs a scavenge pump to return the oil as it collects, and a pressure pump to send it round the engine.

checks.question: Arrange the GTSIO-520 starting torque path.
checks.hint: Torque starts at the starter motor and ends at the crankshaft.
items: Clutch spring grips the shaftgear drum
checks.rationale: The starter turns the worm, the worm turns the worm wheel, the clutch spring tightens onto the wheel hub and grips the shaftgear drum, and the shaftgear drives the crankshaft gear. After the engine starts the spring releases.

checks.question: After the engine starts, what happens to the starter drive?
checks.hint: The starter must not be dragged round by the running engine.
answers: The clutch spring releases, and the shaftgear stays engine-driven
The starter motor must keep driving the crankshaft
A sliding ring-gear pinion disengages from the flywheel
checks.rationale: The spring returns to its normal position and disengages the starter. The shaftgear is then driven by the crankshaft gear. This is a worm and spring adapter, not a sliding pinion.

checks.question: Which value remains unverified in this study?
checks.hint: Two ratios were read from the manual tables. One was not found.
answers: The H fuel-pump drive ratio
The H alternator drive ratio, 3:1
The H tachometer drive ratio, 0.5:1
checks.rationale: The manual tables verify the alternator and tachometer ratios. No numerical fuel-pump drive ratio was established from the passages read, so the model does not state one.

checks.question: Which statement correctly describes the accessory-drives 3D model?
checks.hint: Think about what the model can show and what it cannot.
answers: Drawing-led forms with unscaled sizes and documented drive relationships
Manufacturer dimensions and exact pad positions
IO-520 pump parts that apply automatically to the GTSIO-520-H
checks.rationale: The part forms follow the manufacturer's drawings and the drive relationships are documented, but dimensions, hidden surfaces, teeth, locations and travel are reconstructed, and the IO-520 pump is not used as GTSIO-520-H geometry.

checks.question: Where should a technician get the ignition timing for a particular engine?
checks.hint: A general handbook explains the principle but not every engine's approved setting.
answers: From the manufacturer's data for that engine
From any engine with the same number of cylinders
From the animation in a lesson
checks.rationale: The handbook gives a broad range for the spark before top dead centre across engines and says the ignition must be timed to the engine manufacturer's recommendations. A model or animation cannot authorise a setting.

checks.question: The drive of one magneto fails in flight. What follows?
checks.hint: Remember there are two of every critical ignition unit.
answers: The other ignition system keeps the engine running, with less efficient burning
The engine stops at once because the ignition is shared
Nothing changes, because the two plugs fire together
checks.rationale: Dual ignition has two of every critical unit, so one system can fail without stopping the engine. Lighting the charge at two points burns it more efficiently, so the engine loses some performance when only one system works.

checks.question: Why might an accessory drive shaft include a shear section?
checks.hint: Think about what should break if a pump seizes.
answers: If the accessory seizes, the weak shaft breaks and the rest of the gear train is protected
It lets the accessory run faster than the engine
It reverses the direction of the drive
checks.rationale: A shear section is a deliberately weak shaft. If the pump gears seize, it shears and the rest of the gear train is spared, although the accessory stops working.

checks.question: Tap the alternator.
checks.hint: It makes the aircraft's electricity and sits on its own grey teaching stand in this model.
checks.rationale: The alternator converts shaft power to electrical power. In this study it is shown on a grey teaching stand, and its transfer path is conceptual.

checks.question: Tap a magneto.
checks.hint: There are two of them. Either is a correct answer.
checks.rationale: The engine has two magnetos, each driven through the idler by its own drive gear, one for each of the two ignition systems.

checks.question: Name the highlighted part of the starter drive.
checks.hint: It grips during cranking and lets go once the engine runs.
answers: Wrap-spring clutch
Worm wheel
Starter shaftgear
Idler gear
checks.rationale: This is the starter's wrap-spring clutch. During starting the spring tightens round the drum and carries the motor's torque to the engine; after the engine takes over it releases, so the running engine does not drive the starter.

checks.question: Name the highlighted gear.
checks.hint: It sits between the crankshaft gear and the gears it drives.
answers: Idler gear
Camshaft gear
Crankshaft gear
Fuel pump drive gear
checks.rationale: This is the idler gear. It passes the drive from the crankshaft gear on to other gears; each external mesh reverses the direction, so an idler restores the driver's direction without changing the ratio.

checks.question: Put these in the order the push from the burning gas travels to the propeller.
checks.hint: Start with the gas and end with the shaft the propeller is mounted on.
items: Burning gas pressure on the piston crown
checks.rationale: The gas pushes the piston down, the piston pin passes the push to the connecting rod, the rod pushes on the crankpin so the crankshaft turns, and the crankshaft drives the propeller shaft.

checks.question: Why does the spark fire before the piston reaches top dead centre?
checks.hint: Think about how long burning takes.
answers: Burning takes time, so the charge is lit early enough to be burned completely when the piston is just past TDC
The piston has to be at rest at TDC for the spark plug to work
The exhaust valve is not yet closed at TDC
checks.rationale: The charge is lit before TDC (20° to 35° on various engines) so that combustion is complete when the piston is slightly past TDC and ready to be pushed down.

checks.question: Where should a technician get the ignition timing for a particular engine?
checks.hint: A general handbook explains the principle but not every engine's setting.
answers: From the manufacturer's data for that engine
From any engine with the same number of cylinders
From the animation in a lesson
checks.rationale: The handbook gives a range of 20° to 35° before TDC across various engines and says the ignition must be timed to the engine manufacturer's recommendations. The GTSIO-520 manual gives its own value.

checks.question: What is the compression ratio?
checks.hint: It compares the cylinder's volume with the piston at the two ends of its stroke.
answers: The total cylinder volume with the piston at the bottom divided by the clearance volume with the piston at the top
The crankshaft speed divided by the camshaft speed
The piston displacement divided by the bore diameter
checks.rationale: Compression ratio = total volume (swept volume plus clearance volume) divided by clearance volume. A cylinder with 140 cu in at the bottom and 20 cu in at the top has a ratio of 7 to 1.

checks.question: A cylinder has a swept volume of 80 cu in and a clearance volume of 10 cu in. What is its compression ratio? Give the first number of the ratio, for example 8 for 8:1.
checks.hint: Total volume = swept volume + clearance volume.
checks.rationale: Total volume is 80 + 10 = 90 cu in, and 90 ÷ 10 = 9, so the compression ratio is 9:1.

checks.question: One cylinder of the GTSIO-520-H has a bore of 5.250 in and a stroke of 4.000 in. What is its piston displacement, to the nearest tenth of a cubic inch?
checks.hint: Area of the piston = 0.7854 × bore squared; displacement = area × stroke.
checks.rationale: 0.7854 × 5.25² = 21.65 sq in, and 21.65 × 4.00 = 86.6 cu in. Six cylinders give 519.5 cu in, the 520 cu in in the engine's name.

checks.question: The GTSIO-520-H has a compression ratio of 7.5:1 and a swept volume of 86.6 cu in per cylinder. What is the clearance volume, to the nearest tenth of a cubic inch?
checks.hint: Compression ratio = (swept + clearance) ÷ clearance, so swept ÷ clearance = ratio - 1.
checks.rationale: Clearance volume = swept volume ÷ (compression ratio - 1) = 86.6 ÷ 6.5 = 13.3 cu in. The total volume is then 86.6 + 13.3 = 99.9 cu in.

checks.question: Which of these describes detonation?
checks.hint: In the other abnormal case the burning starts before the spark.
answers: The spark plug lights the charge, but it explodes instead of burning at a controlled rate
The charge starts to burn before the spark plug fires
The charge fails to burn at all
checks.rationale: In detonation the spark lights the charge but it explodes, so the cylinder temperature and pressure spike. Burning that starts before the spark is pre-ignition.

checks.question: Why are the gaps of a piston's rings staggered round the piston?
checks.hint: Think about a straight path for gas.
answers: So gas that gets past one ring meets a solid part of the next, which keeps blow-by down
So the rings are easier to push into the cylinder
So the piston weighs the same on both sides
checks.rationale: Staggered gaps do not line up, so there is no straight path for gas to leak past the piston. If they line up, blow-by and oil burning increase.

checks.question: Match each rule from the GTSIO-520 assembly pages to what it says.
checks.hint: Each rule is about position or order.

pairs.right: Tightened in the manual's sequence to the value in its limits chapter
Alternate rings have their gaps 180° apart

pairs.left: Position number on the piston head
pairs.right: Faces the front of the engine
Fitted first, so the crankshaft is turned as little as possible

checks.rationale: These are the manual's own assembly rules: staggered ring gaps, the piston numbered forward, the order that keeps the crankshaft balanced, and torque in sequence to the manual value.

checks.question: Before a cylinder is removed, where should its valve lifters be?
checks.hint: Think about where the cam is not pushing.
answers: On the heels of their cam lobes, with both valves fully closed
At the top of their cam lobes, with both valves open
Removed from the crankcase first
checks.rationale: The crankshaft is positioned so the lifters rest on the heels (base circles) of the lobes and both valves are closed, so nothing is under spring load when the rocker assemblies and pushrods come off.

checks.question: Put these stages of the energy chain in order, from the fuel to the end.
checks.hint: Start with the chemical energy in the fuel and end with the force that moves the aircraft.
items: Shaft power at the propeller shaft
checks.rationale: The fuel burns to make heat, the heat raises the gas pressure, the pressure pushes on the piston, the crankshaft turns the push into torque, torque at a speed is shaft power, and the propeller turns shaft power into thrust.

checks.question: What three things must come together for the fuel's energy to be released?
checks.hint: One supplies the energy, one the oxygen and one starts the burn.
answers: Fuel, air and ignition
Fuel, oil and ignition
Air, oil and compression
Fuel, air and cooling
checks.rationale: The fuel supplies the energy, the air supplies the oxygen it burns in, and the ignition starts the burn at the right moment. Without any one of them, no energy is released.

checks.question: The gas pressure on a piston is 500 psi and the piston has an area of 20 square inches. What force pushes on the piston?
checks.hint: Force is pressure times area.
checks.rationale: 500 psi × 20 in² = 10,000 lb. A larger piston or a higher pressure gives a larger force.

checks.question: A push of 150 lb acts at right angles on an arm 2 ft long. What torque does it give?
checks.hint: Torque is the force times its distance from the axis.
checks.rationale: 150 lb × 2 ft = 300 lb-ft. Torque is measured in pound-feet, which should not be confused with work in foot-pounds.

checks.question: An engine delivers a torque of 500 lb-ft at 2,500 rpm. What brake horsepower is that? Use bhp = 2π × torque × rpm ÷ 33,000 and give the answer to the nearest whole number.
checks.hint: Multiply 2π (6.2832) by the torque and the rpm, then divide by 33,000.
checks.rationale: 6.2832 × 500 × 2,500 ÷ 33,000 = 238 hp. The same power would come from a lower torque at a higher speed.

checks.question: An engine delivers 300 brake horsepower to a propeller that is 80 percent efficient. How much thrust horsepower does the combination give?
checks.hint: Thrust horsepower is the brake horsepower times the propeller efficiency.
checks.rationale: 300 × 0.80 = 240 thrust horsepower. The propeller never converts all of the shaft power into thrust power.

checks.question: What is the difference between indicated horsepower and brake horsepower?
checks.hint: One is measured in the cylinders and the other at the propeller shaft.
answers: The friction horsepower: the power used to overcome friction and to drive the pumps and other accessories
The power lost in the propeller
The power lost in the exhaust only
There is no difference in a modern engine
checks.rationale: Indicated horsepower is developed in the cylinders. Friction, drawing in fuel, expelling exhaust and driving the oil and fuel pumps and other accessories take some of it, as much as 10 to 15 percent, and the rest is the brake horsepower delivered to the propeller.

checks.question: Match each aircraft service to the kind of power it uses.
checks.hint: Think about what the accessory moves: electrons, air or fluid.

pairs.right: Electrical
Pneumatic
Hydraulic

checks.rationale: The alternator makes electrical power, the vacuum pump makes a pneumatic supply (suction), and an engine-driven pump supplies a hydraulic system. In each case the engine turns the accessory, so the service takes engine power indirectly.

checks.question: Match each part of the power-generating assembly to its job.
checks.hint: Follow the push from the gas to the propeller shaft.

pairs.right: Takes the push of the burning gas
Seal the gas and control the oil
Carries the push to the crankpin
Changes the back-and-forth motion into rotation
Carries the valves and the spark plugs

checks.rationale: The piston takes the gas force, its rings seal the gas, the connecting rod passes the push to the off-centre crankpin, the crankshaft turns it into rotation, and the cylinder head carries the valves and spark plugs.

checks.question: Tap the connecting rod.
checks.hint: It links the piston pin to the crankpin.
checks.rationale: The connecting rod carries the push from the piston, through the piston pin, to the crankpin. Its cap, bolts and bearing halves are separate parts.

checks.question: Tap the piston.
checks.hint: It is the part that slides in the cylinder and receives the push of the gas.
checks.rationale: The piston takes the force of the burning gas on its crown. Its rings and pin are separate parts.

checks.question: A six-cylinder four-stroke engine has its power events evenly spaced through the cycle. How many degrees of crankshaft rotation are there between one power event and the next?
checks.hint: The cycle takes 720° of crankshaft rotation. Share it among the cylinders.
checks.rationale: 720° ÷ 6 cylinders = 120° between power events.

checks.question: A four-cylinder four-stroke engine has its power events evenly spaced through the cycle. How many degrees of crankshaft rotation are there between one power event and the next?
